Evolution of NBA Playing Styles: A Data-Driven Analysis¶

0. What is the NBA?¶

The National Basketball Association (NBA) is the world’s premier professional basketball league, featuring thirty teams from major cities across the United States and Canada. Since its founding in 1946, the NBA has grown into a global cultural phenomenon, showcasing some of the greatest athletic talents and most innovative playing styles the sport has ever seen. Beyond its annual championship races and star-studded All-Star events, the league continually pushes the envelope in rulemaking, technology, and fan engagement—setting trends that resonate through amateur, collegiate, and international basketball. As it evolves, the NBA remains both a competitive sporting enterprise and a cultural touchstone, making it an ideal subject for rigorous, data-driven exploration.

1. Project Overview¶

Over the past four decades, the NBA has undergone a dramatic transformation. What was once a league dominated by back-to-the-basket centers and midrange specialists is now defined by pace, space, and an unprecedented reliance on the three-point shot.

In an era where virtually every aspect of basketball can be measured—from how players move on the court to the efficiency of each shot attempt—simply watching the game is no longer enough to understand its deeper patterns and trends. A thoughtful, data-driven analysis transforms raw numbers into meaningful insights, revealing the subtle shifts in playing styles, team strategies, and overall league dynamics that aren’t always obvious in the box score or the highlight reel. By systematically examining decades of statistical records, we gain a clearer picture of how the sport has evolved and why certain approaches succeed or falter. Moreover, such an analytical framework serves as a guiding compass for everyone involved in the basketball ecosystem. For practitioners—coaches, managers, and trainers—it offers an objective foundation for decision-making, helping to shape practice priorities, roster construction, and in-game adjustments. For the league itself, it provides a lens through which to assess the impact of past changes and to anticipate future developments. And for fans and storytellers, it enriches the narrative, turning every arc of a trajectory, every trend line, into a chapter in basketball’s ongoing story. Ultimately, this project does more than look backward; it lights the path forward. By uncovering persistent patterns and emerging tendencies, we equip the sport’s stakeholders with the foresight to adapt, innovate, and continue elevating the game. In doing so, we help ensure that basketball’s next phase—wherever it may lead—is informed, deliberate, and full of fresh possibilities.

2. Core Objectives¶

At its core, this work pursues four interrelated goals:

  1. Measure Stylistic Shifts: Quantify how league-wide pace, shot distributions, and three-point usage have trended since the late 1970s.
  2. Identify Driving Forces: Investigate the forces behind these shifts—rule changes (like the three-point line or hand-checking bans), the emergence of transcendent players, and evolving coaching philosophies.
  3. Define Stylistic Archetypes: Cluster teams and eras into distinct stylistic groups, revealing, for example, when “pace-and-space” became a dominant blueprint and which franchises bucked prevailing trends.
  4. Forecast Future Developments: Project how the next chapter of basketball strategy may unfold in shooting and tempo using time-series forecasting.

3. The Datasets¶

To achieve these aims, we draw on multiple rich datasets:

  • Advanced.csv: Player-level advanced metrics, providing per-season measurements such as true shooting percentage and usage rate.
  • league_season_summary.csv: Team summaries capturing aggregate trends in pace and offensive efficiency.
  • team_season_3pt_share.csv: Tracks each franchise’s three-point attempt rate over time.
  • shots_sampled.csv: A sampled shot-level dataset adding spatial detail—shot coordinates, defender proximity, and make/miss outcomes—for fine-grained analysis of shot quality.

4. Analytical Approach¶

Our methodology unfolds in four distinct stages:

  1. Data Cleaning & Preparation: Thoroughly clean and normalize the data, resolving missing values and aligning season definitions across files.
  2. Descriptive Analytics & Visualization: Use time-series and spatial visualizations (e.g., shot charts, heatmaps) to sketch the broad contours of the league’s stylistic evolution.
  3. Clustering & Dimensionality Reduction: Apply techniques such as K-Means Clustering and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to distill team-season profiles into interpretable stylistic clusters.
  4. Predictive Modeling: Employ logistic regression (to model shot success) and time-series forecasting (to project future pace and three-point share) to quantify how trends might continue.

5. Conclusion & Impact¶

By weaving together exploratory analysis, clustering, and forecasting, this project not only documents the NBA’s past but equips analysts, coaches, and fans with tools to anticipate its future. In translating raw statistics into a coherent narrative, we hope to illuminate the dynamics that have reshaped basketball—from the corner three’s rise to the fall of the midrange jumper—and to offer data-driven insights that could shape the next era of the game.

Dataset 1 – NBA Advanced Player Statistics (player_stats_advanced.csv)¶

We rely on the public NBA player statistics archive from Kaggle, focusing on the Advanced Statistics file.

It delivers a season-by-season accounting of every player’s impact metrics, allowing us to track the league’s stylistic heartbeat across 78 years.

Structure of the dataset¶

  • Observations: One row per player-season ($\approx 32,000$ total).
  • Time span: 1946-47 BAA debut $\rightarrow$ 2024-25 NBA season.
  • Leagues: BAA ’46-49 | NBA ’49-present | ABA ’67-76 (merged ’76-77).
  • Teams & franchises: All historical logos; name changes preserved (e.g., Seattle $\rightarrow$ OKC).
  • File size: ~6 MB CSV, 40+ columns, UTF-8, comma-delimited.

Main variables (subset we extract)¶

  • Efficiency: ts_percent, e_fg_percent
    • Purpose: Track scoring floor/ceiling.
  • Shot diet: x3p_ar, f_tr
    • Purpose: Quantify perimeter vs paint emphasis.
  • Usage & creation: usg_percent, ast_percent, tov_percent
    • Purpose: Separate engines from finishers.
  • Impact composites: per, bpm, obpm, dbpm, ws, ws_48, vorp
    • Purpose: Tie stylistic change to wins.
  • Role splits: orb_percent, drb_percent, stl_percent, blk_percent
    • Purpose: Reveal positional responsibilities.
  • Identifiers: player, season, team, pos, league, mp
    • Purpose: Merge keys & minute anchor.

Why this dataset?¶

  • Era breadth – covers every major rules epoch (shot-clock, 3-pt line, hand-check ban, etc.).
  • Analytics focus – metrics are already pace- & minute-adjusted $\rightarrow$ instant comparability.
  • Front-office parity – mirrors the stats NBA analytics staffs debate (TS%, BPM, VORP).
  • Clean CSV – loads directly into Pandas; perfect for clustering, panel regression, PCA.
  • Open license – Kaggle hosting ensures reproducibility without API throttles.

Analytical opportunities¶

  • Long-run trends: 3PAr, FTr, TS% across decades.
  • Role evolution: big-men vs. guards usage & efficiency shifts.
  • Positionless analysis: cluster player-seasons by (height, 3PAr, AST%).
  • Rule-change impacts: ABA merger, hand-check ban, freedom-of-movement emphasis.
  • Efficiency vs. volume trade-offs: USG% vs TS% curves by era.

In summary, this table gives us a bird’s-eye measure of what changed (usage, efficiency, role) across nearly eight decades—forming the backbone for all non-spatial analyses.

Dataset 2 – NBA Shot-Level Geometry Ledger (season_shots_1997_2025.csv)¶

To uncover where the revolution happened on the floor, we scrape the NBA Stats API’s ShotChartDetail endpoint and cache the result to a tidy CSV.

The file logs every regular-season field-goal attempt from 1996-97 to 2024-25, capturing the spatial DNA of roughly 2.6 million shots.

Structure of the dataset¶

  • Observations: One row per shot attempt (make or miss).
  • Time span: 1996-97 $\rightarrow$ 2024-25 (29 seasons).
  • Granularity: Regular-season only; playoffs excluded to avoid small-sample bias.
  • Columns: 22 raw fields + engineered tags (see below).
  • File size: ~200 MB CSV, float-safe, comma-delimited.

Main variables (native + engineered)¶

  • Spatial: loc_x, loc_y, shot_distance
    • Purpose: XY geometry in feet for heat-maps & zone tags.
  • Shot label: shot_type, shot_zone_basic, $\rightarrow$ zone3 (corner/above-break tag)
    • Purpose: Classify 2P vs 3P + detailed zones.
  • Context: period, game_clock, shot_clock
    • Purpose: Split transition vs half-court, clutch, etc.
  • Identifiers: player_id, team_id, game_id, $\rightarrow$ season
    • Purpose: Merge with advanced panel & lineup subs.
  • Temporal: game_date, matchup
    • Purpose: Study back-to-backs, home/away efficiency.

(Engineered after load: zone3, restricted-area flag, hex-bin grid indices, lineup hull-area.)

Why this dataset?¶

  • Unique XY coverage – the only free, league-official source with full-court coordinates pre-2013.
  • Granularity – row-level detail lets us aggregate upward (player, lineup, season) on demand.
  • Spatial storytelling – enables corner-three counts, distance histograms, spacing indices.
  • Reproducibility – local CSV avoids API rate limits; same row counts every run.
  • Complementarity – links directly to the advanced panel (season, player_id) for hybrid models.

Analytical opportunities¶

  • Corner vs above-break trends (1997-2025).
  • Hex-bin efficiency maps by era or team.
  • Lineup spacing index: convex-hull area of off-ball positions.
  • Pull-up vs catch-and-shoot splits via shot-clock & distance filters.
  • Event studies: effect of hand-check ban on average shot distance.

In summary, this ledger supplies the where and how far of every jumper in the modern era—fueling every geography-based insight, from corner-three scarcity to the rise of 28-ft pull-ups.

Research Questions¶

1) Era Comparison — “Who Would Dominate?”¶

We ask:¶

$$ \text{How do pace- and league-adjusted player statistics differ across historical eras?} $$

Formal setup¶

Raw metric for player $i$ in season $t$: $x_{i,t}$ (e.g., $\text{TS\%}$).

Pace-adjusted per-100-possessions value: $$ x^{*}_{i,t}=\frac{x_{i,t}}{P_t}\times 100, $$ with $P_t$ = league possessions / game.

Z-score within season: $$ z_{i,t}=\frac{x^{*}_{i,t}-\mu_t}{\sigma_t}. $$

Statistical comparison¶

  • Null: decade-level $z_{i,t}$ distributions are identical.
  • Tests: two-sample KS ($D$), Welch $t$, Mann–Whitney $U$.
  • Effect size: Cohen’s $d=\dfrac{\bar{x}_A-\bar{x}_B}{s_p}$.

Mathematical / Statistical references¶

Sampling-distribution theory for two-sample tests; non-parametric rank tests for unequal variances; effect-size interpretation thresholds ($|d| > 0.8$ ≈ “large”).

What we explore & how¶

Create violin & box plots of $z_{i,t}$ by decade, annotate test statistics, then highlight which eras truly separate after correcting for pace and offensive environment. The visuals plus $d$ quantify whether “Wilt-era dominance” survives modern context-balancing.

2) Positionless Basketball — “Do Bigs Look Like Guards?”¶

We ask:¶

$$ \text{Have modern PF/Cs converged toward guards in shot selection and playmaking?} $$

Formal setup¶

Player-season feature vector: $$ \mathbf{x}_{i,t}=[\text{3PA},\;\text{FTA},\;\text{3P\%},\;\text{AST\%},\;\text{TOV\%},\;\text{USG\%},\;\text{DRB\%},\;\text{BLK\%}]. $$

Statistical comparison¶

  • Dimensionality reduction: PCA on $X^{\top}X$ $\rightarrow$ 2-D.
  • Clustering: $k$-means, $k=3$–5, repeated 100$\times$ for stability.
  • Overlap metric: silhouette score by true position labels.

Mathematical / Statistical references¶

Eigen-decomposition for PCA; Lloyd’s algorithm for $k$-means; silhouette index ($s\in[-1,1]$) as cluster-separation gauge.

What we explore & how¶

Scatter-plot first two PCs per season bucket (1990s $\rightarrow$ 2020s) with guard vs. big colors. A rising silhouette score toward 0 signals positional blending. We’ll narrate specific inflection years (e.g., 2013 “small-ball” playoff revolution).

3) Career Longevity Prediction — “Who Lasts 10+ Years?”¶

We ask:¶

$$ \text{Which rookie-contract statistics forecast a ≥10-season NBA career?} $$

Formal setup¶

Binary target: $$ Y_i=\begin{cases}1,&\text{career}\ge 10\\[2pt]0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}, $$ predictors = rookie-year counting & rate stats.

Statistical comparison¶

  • Model: logistic regression $$ \Pr(Y_i=1|\mathbf{x}_i)=\sigma(\beta_0+\mathbf{x}_i^\top\beta). $$
  • Validation: stratified 5-fold CV; metrics = AUC, F1.
  • Interpretability: permutation importance + partial-dependence plots.

Mathematical / Statistical references¶

Maximum-likelihood estimation for logistic models; ROC-curve analysis; permutation-based feature relevance (Breiman 2001).

What we explore & how¶

Fit the model on 1979-2020 cohorts, visualize top five early indicators (e.g., AST% & VORP). A “what-if” slider demo (PDP) illustrates marginal impact on survival probability.

4) Cross-Era Archetypes — “What Roles Exist and How They Shift”¶

We ask:¶

$$ \text{How do data-driven player archetypes change definition and prevalence over decades?} $$

Formal setup¶

  • Standardize features $\{\text{PTS},\text{AST},\text{TRB},\text{STL},\text{BLK},\text{3PA},\text{3P\%},\text{USG\%}\}$.
  • PCA $\Rightarrow$ retain first $q$ PCs (85% variance).
  • $k$-means on PC scores, $k=4$ (“Rim Protector”, “3&D Wing”, “Initiator”, “Stretch Big”).
  • Prevalence per decade: $$ \pi_{k,d}=\frac{|\{i\ \text{in cluster }k\text{ during }d\}|}{|\{\text{all players in }d\}|}. $$
  • Centroid drift: $$ \Delta_k(d_1,d_2)=\|\mu_{k,d_1}-\mu_{k,d_2}\|_2. $$

Statistical comparison¶

ANOVA on PC space tests whether centroids shift significantly ($p<0.05$).

Mathematical / Statistical references¶

Between-group sum-of-squares in $k$-means; Hotelling’s $T^2$ for centroid change.

What we explore & how¶

Stacked-area plot of $\pi_{k,d}$ shows the wave of Stretch Bigs post-2012. Heat-map of $\Delta_k$ pinpoints which archetype’s “center of gravity” moved farthest (spoiler: Initiators drift to higher 3PA).

5) The Long-Range Revolution — “How Far Have We Stretched the Floor?”¶

We ask:¶

$$ \text{Does average shot distance predict league TS\% increases?} $$

Formal setup¶

$$ d_t=\frac{1}{N_t}\sum_{i}\text{SHOT\_DISTANCE}_{i,t},\qquad e_t=\text{TS\%}_t. $$

Statistical comparison¶

  • OLS: $e_t=\beta_0+\beta_1 d_t+\varepsilon_t$.
  • First-difference robustness: $\Delta e_t$ vs. $\Delta d_t$.
  • Durbin-Watson tests autocorrelation.

Mathematical / Statistical references¶

OLS assumptions; Newey-West HAC if residuals exhibit AR(1).

What we explore & how¶

Twin-axis line chart of $d_t$ & $e_t$ (1979–2025) plus regression table. If $\beta_1\approx 0.4$ TS-pts per extra foot, we’ll credit range-stretching as a direct efficiency lever.

6) Positionless Basketball — “Do Bigs Now Shoot Like Guards?”¶

We ask:¶

$$ \text{Have PF/Cs adopted guard-level three-point volume and shot profile?} $$

Formal setup¶

$$ \mathbf{x}_{i,t}=[\text{3PA},\;\text{3PAr},\;\text{AST\%},\;\text{USG\%},\;\text{DRB\%},\;\text{BLK\%}]. $$

Statistical comparison¶

  • PCA $\rightarrow$ 2-D.
  • $k$-means ($k=2$) labels “Guard-style” vs. “Interior-style”.
  • Track yearly share of PF/Cs falling into Guard-style cluster.

Mathematical / Statistical references¶

Silhouette vs. Calinski-Harabasz to justify $k=2$; logistic-time trend for adoption curve.

What we explore & how¶

Animated scatter (1997→2025) shows bigs migrating into the guard cloud. Adoption curve quantifies the inflection (~2016) powered by Stretch 5 specialists.

7) Anatomy of the Three — “Corner vs. Above-the-Break”¶

We ask:¶

$$ \text{Which three-point zone ignited the volume explosion, and with what efficiency payoff?} $$

Formal setup¶

$$ c_t=\frac{\#\text{corner-3}_t}{N_t},\quad a_t=\frac{\#\text{above-break-3}_t}{N_t},\quad \eta_c,\eta_a=\text{mean 3P\% by zone}. $$ Expected points per 3PA: $E[P_{3,t}]=3(c_t\eta_c+a_t\eta_a)$.

Statistical comparison¶

  • Slopes $\frac{dc_t}{dt}$ & $\frac{da_t}{dt}$ pre/post 2010.
  • Chow test for structural break (2008 hand-check rule changes).
  • Correlate $E[P_{3,t}]$ with league ORtg.

Mathematical / Statistical references¶

Zone-based efficiency decomposition; structural-break econometrics.

What we explore & how¶

Plot $c_t$, $a_t$, $\eta_c$, $\eta_a$ together. Expect corner share plateau (~2018) while above-break keeps rising, implying teams mined the low-hanging 22-ft gold first.

8) Speed Meets Spacing — “Is Pace the Secret Sauce?”¶

We ask:¶

$$ \text{Do seasons combining high pace and long average distance yield the biggest ORtg jumps?} $$

Formal setup¶

$$ \text{ORtg}_t=\beta_0+\beta_1 d_t+\beta_2 p_t+\varepsilon_t, $$ $d_t$ = avg shot distance, $p_t$ = pace.

Statistical comparison¶

  • Compare $R^2$ base vs. full model.
  • Interaction term $d_t \cdot p_t$ tests synergy.
  • Semi-partial correlations parse unique contribution.

Mathematical / Statistical references¶

Variance-decomposition in multiple regression; interaction-effect interpretation.

What we explore & how¶

3-D surface (p, d, ORtg) reveals a ridge: high-pace, spread-floor seasons (e.g., 2021) sit at the summit. We’ll rank top-5 “speed-plus-spacing” seasons.

9) Early Adopters — “Crossing the 40 % Three-Point Threshold”¶

We ask:¶

$$ \text{Which franchises first crossed 40 % 3PA share and how did efficiency respond?} $$

Formal setup¶

$$ s_{k,t}=\frac{\#\text{3PA}_{k,t}}{\#\text{FGA}_{k,t}},\qquad t_k^{*}=\min\{t:s_{k,t}>0.4\},\qquad \Delta e_k=e_{k,t_k^{*}+1}-e_{k,t_k^{*}-1}. $$

Statistical comparison¶

Paired $t$-test of pre- vs. post-threshold TS%; league-adjust the efficiency delta to isolate team effect.

Mathematical / Statistical references¶

Difference-in-differences framing; small-sample paired testing.

What we explore & how¶

Timeline chart marking each team’s $t_k^{*}$, plus bar plot of $\Delta e_k$. Expect early Houston / Moreyball era to show $\ge 2$ TS-pts surge, validating bold strategic pivots.

10) The Mid-Range Floor — “Is the Pull-Up Dead or Stabilized?”¶

We ask:¶

$$ \text{Has mid-range attempt share $m_t$ decayed to zero or settled to a non-zero floor?} $$

Formal setup¶

$$ m_t=\frac{\#\text{mid-range}_t}{N_t},\qquad t=1997,\dots,2025. $$

Statistical comparison¶

  • Piece-wise linear: slopes $\beta_1$ (pre-2015) vs. $\beta_2$ (post-2015).
  • Exponential fit $m_0e^{-\lambda t}$; test $\lambda>0$ but $m_t\not\to 0$.
  • Forecast 2030 share with ARIMA for stationarity check.

Mathematical / Statistical references¶

Structural-break (Chow) test; nonlinear least squares for exponential decay; ARIMA diagnostics (ADF, Ljung–Box).

What we explore & how¶

Line plot with fitted curves shows steep fall through 2015, then flattening ~7% FGA. A persistent floor would suggest defenses still conceding mid-range or certain stars (e.g., Durant) preserving the art.

11) The Expanding Shot Geography¶

We ask: $$ \text{How did the spatial distribution of field-goal attempts evolve across eras, and what statistical evidence captures this shift?} $$

Formal setup.¶

Let $s_{z,t}$ denote the share of shots from zone $z \in \{\text{Rim}, \text{Mid-Range}, \text{Three-Point}\}$ in season $t$. We define: $$ s_{z,t} = \frac{N_{z,t}}{N_t}, $$ where $N_{z,t}$ is the total number of attempts from zone $z$, and $N_t$ is the total number of league attempts that season.

Statistical comparison.¶

  • Compute $\Delta s_{z,t} = s_{z,t} - s_{z,t-1}$ to track annual rate of change.
  • Fit a linear regression $s_{z,t} = \alpha_z + \beta_z t + \varepsilon_t$ to quantify long-term directional trends.
  • Visualize as stacked areas to express zero-sum zone migration.

Mathematical/Statistical References.¶

The analysis treats the league's shot diet as a vector of proportions where $\sum_z s_{z,t} = 1$, imposing a zero-sum constraint. The regression $s_{z,t} = \alpha_z + \beta_z t + \varepsilon_t$ is a linear time-trend model, where the coefficient $\beta_z$ represents the average absolute change in shot share per season, and its $t$-statistic tests against the null hypothesis of a static shot distribution ($H_0: \beta_z = 0$).

What we explore & how.¶

We're tracking the "market share" of each shot zone over the last 30 years. The stacked area chart will be the key visual, as it will perfectly show how the mid-range's share (e.g., 45% of all shots) was "eaten" by the three-point line's share (which grew from 15% to 40%), while the rim's share remained steady. The regression simply puts a hard number on this: we'll find a $\beta_{\text{mid}} \approx -0.9$ and $\beta_{\text{three}} \approx +0.9$, proving the "Great Migration" was a one-for-one trade.

12) Efficiency $\times$ Volume: How Shot-Mix Powered the NBA’s Scoring Boom¶

We ask: $$ \text{Can changes in shot distribution alone explain the rise in league shooting efficiency (TS\%)?} $$

Formal setup.¶

Let $v_t^{(3)}$ and $v_t^{(\text{mid})}$ denote the three-point and mid-range attempt shares in season $t$, and $y_t$ the league-wide true shooting percentage. We model: $$ y_t = \alpha + \beta_1 v_t^{(3)} + \beta_2 v_t^{(\text{mid})} + \varepsilon_t. $$

Statistical comparison.¶

  • Estimate via OLS and compute correlation coefficients.
  • Evaluate $R^2$ to assess explanatory power of volume redistribution on efficiency growth.
  • Interpret $\beta_1 > 0$ and $\beta_2 < 0$ as empirical support for the “shot-mix efficiency” hypothesis.

Mathematical/Statistical References.¶

This is a multivariate linear regression (OLS) model. The coefficient of determination ($R^2$) will be the key metric, quantifying the proportion of variance in league TS% that is statistically explained by shot-mix alone. The partial regression coefficients ($\beta_1, \beta_2$) will test our one-sided hypotheses ($H_A: \beta_1 > 0$, $H_A: \beta_2 < 0$), confirming the direction and magnitude of each zone's impact on efficiency.

What we explore & how.¶

This is the "Moreyball" hypothesis test. We already proved where the shots moved (Q11); now we're proving why it mattered. We'll run a regression with league TS% as the dependent variable and the 3PA%/Mid% shares as the predictors. A high $R^2$ (e.g., > 0.85) will be our smoking gun, proving that the scoring boom wasn't just "better shooters" but a structural change in shot selection. We fully expect to find $\beta_1$ (threes) is strongly positive and $\beta_2$ (mid-range) is strongly negative.

13) The Rise of Playmaking Bigs: Redefining Roles in the Modern NBA¶

We ask: $$ \text{How has the assist creation and ball-handling responsibility of frontcourt players evolved since the early 2000s?} $$

Formal setup.¶

Let $a_{p,t}$ denote the average assist percentage (AST%) for players at position $p \in \{\text{Guard}, \text{Forward}, \text{Center}\}$ in season $t$. Compute: $$ \Delta a_{p,t} = a_{p,t} - a_{\text{Guard},t}, $$ as the assist-gap between each position and traditional guards.

Statistical comparison.¶

  • Use trend regressions and moving averages on $a_{p,t}$ to measure role convergence.
  • Hypothesis: $\text{Var}_p(a_{p,t})$ (the variance between positional averages) decreases over time, signaling “positionless” creation.

Mathematical/Statistical References.¶

The primary test is for statistical convergence. We hypothesize that the cross-sectional variance of the positional means, $\text{Var}_p(a_{p,t})$, follows a negative time trend. By plotting $a_{p,t}$ for all $p$ on one chart, we can visually test for this convergence. The $\Delta a_{p,t}$ metric simply baselines the data against the "traditional playmaker" role, making the narrowing gap easier to interpret.

What we explore & how.¶

We're quantifying the "Nikola Jokic" or "Point-Center" effect. We'll plot the average AST% for Guards, Forwards, and Centers on a single line chart from 1990 to 2025. We expect to see the "Guard" line stay relatively flat, while the "Forward" and "Center" lines show a clear upward trend, converging toward the guard line. This visual convergence is the clearest evidence of positional blending and the rise of playmaking bigs, moving the league from specialized roles to a more "positionless" model.

14) Corner vs. Above-Break: Deconstructing the 3-Point Boom¶

We ask: $$ \text{Which region—corner or above-break—drove the long-range revolution in accuracy and volume?} $$

Formal setup.¶

Let $c_t$ and $a_t$ denote the fraction of league three-point attempts from corner and above-break zones, and $\eta_c, \eta_a$ their respective efficiencies (3P%). We compute: $$ \text{Expected Points per 3PA}_t = 3 \times (c_t \eta_c + a_t \eta_a). $$

Statistical comparison.¶

  • Analyze trends in $c_t$ and $a_t$ over time.
  • Compare slopes $\frac{d c_t}{dt}$ and $\frac{d a_t}{dt}$ pre- and post-2010.
  • Interpret their contributions to league-wide offensive rating growth.

Mathematical/Statistical References.¶

The $\text{Expected Points}$ formula is a weighted average, a direct application of Expected Value (EV) theory. The comparison of $\frac{d c_t}{dt}$ (the derivative, or slope, of corner-three share over time) and $\frac{d a_t}{dt}$ (the slope of above-break share) is a comparative rate-of-change analysis, allowing us to determine which component provided the greater marginal increase in volume.

What we explore & how.¶

We're drilling down into the 3-point boom. Everyone knows the corner three is efficient, but is it the driver of the volume? We'll split all 3-pointers into two buckets ("Corner" vs. "Above-Break") and plot their shares of the total 3PA pie over time. This will likely reveal a counter-intuitive story: the share of threes from the "efficient" corner has stayed small and relatively flat, while the "less efficient" above-the-break pull-up has truly exploded, proving the revolution was driven by volume and pull-up skill, not just by optimizing for the corner.

from nba_api.stats.endpoints import shotchartdetail
import pandas as pd
import time, json
from tqdm.notebook import tqdm   # progress bar

# -------------------------------------------
# 2.  Helper: download one season
# -------------------------------------------
def fetch_season_shots(season_str: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """
    Download *all* regular-season shot attempts for one NBA season.
    season_str has the form '1996-97', '2024-25', etc.
    """
    resp = shotchartdetail.ShotChartDetail(
        team_id              = 0,            # 0 = all teams
        player_id            = 0,            # 0 = all players
        season_nullable      = season_str,
        season_type_all_star = 'Regular Season',
        context_measure_simple = 'FGA'       # return made + missed shots :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
    )

    # Convert raw JSON (headers + rowSet) → DataFrame
    data   = json.loads(resp.get_json())['resultSets'][0]
    df     = pd.DataFrame(data['rowSet'], columns=data['headers'])  # :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}
    df['SEASON_ID'] = season_str       # keep a clean season key
    return df

# -------------------------------------------
# 3.  Download all seasons (may take ~3-4 min)
# -------------------------------------------
seasons   = [f"{yr}-{str(yr+1)[-2:]}" for yr in range(1996, 2025)]
all_dfs   = []

for s in tqdm(seasons, desc="Downloading"):
    try:
        all_dfs.append(fetch_season_shots(s))
        time.sleep(0.6)   # polite pause to avoid rate limits
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  {s}: {e}")

shots_raw = pd.concat(all_dfs, ignore_index=True)

# -------------------------------------------
# 4.  Basic cleaning that you’ll build on later
# -------------------------------------------
numeric_cols = ['LOC_X', 'LOC_Y', 'SHOT_DISTANCE']
shots_raw[numeric_cols] = shots_raw[numeric_cols].astype(float)

shots_raw['Season'] = shots_raw['SEASON_ID'].str[:4].astype(int) + 1  # align with advanced.csv
shots_raw = shots_raw[shots_raw['PLAYER_ID'] != 'PLAYER_ID']          # drop any rogue header rows

# -------------------------------------------
# 5.  Persist to disk
# -------------------------------------------
shots_raw.to_csv('season_shots_1997_2025.csv', index=False)
print(" Saved season_shots_1997_2025.csv — rows:", len(shots_raw))

2) Data-Cleaning & Sampling Phase – what we changed and why it matters¶

A. Scrubbing and enriching the player-season table (Advanced.csv)¶

  • Step: Season strings $\rightarrow$ four-digit year

    • Code snippet: season_to_year("1999-00") $\rightarrow$ 2000
    • Practical reason: NBA season IDs are stored in mixed formats (1999‐00, 1997, integers). Unifying them to a single integer lets us merge seamlessly with other season-based tables and create decade buckets.

  • Step: Force numerics

    • Code snippet: pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce") on ~25 stat columns
    • Practical reason: Safely converts “—”, empty strings, or odd characters to NaN instead of crashing later math. Ensures every stat column is truly numeric for correlation, regression, etc.

  • Step: League filter

    • Code snippet: df[df["lg"].isin(["NBA","ABA","BAA"])]
    • Practical reason: Removes stray rows (e.g., college, exhibition, G-League) that would dilute pro-level trends.

  • Step: Duplicate purge

    • Code snippet: drop_duplicates(["player_id","player","season","team","mp"])
    • Practical reason: Some players change teams mid-season; data scrapes can double-count those lines. Keeping one record per (player, season, team, minutes) avoids inflating sample size.

  • Step: Position simplification

    • Code snippet: pos_simple("PF-C") $\rightarrow$ "C"
    • Practical reason: Condenses hybrid strings into a single letter G/F/C. This sacrifices granularity but prevents tiny sub-classes from fragmenting box-plots and group means.

  • Step: Era label

    • Code snippet: era(2005) $\rightarrow$ "2000s"
    • Practical reason: Creates decade buckets that are easier for non-statistical readers to follow than raw years.

  • Step: Minutes buckets & “core” sample

    • Code snippet: pd.cut(mp, …) and df_core = df[df["mp"] >= 500]
    • Practical reason: Low-minute stints (< 500 MP) often have noisy rate stats. The core filter keeps meaningful contributors while mp_bucket preserves the option to study usage tiers later.

Net result: a tidy df and a high-quality df_core that power the histograms, box-plots, and correlations we built in the EDA section.

B. RAM-safe streaming pipeline for 23 M+ shot events (season_shots_1997_2025.csv)¶

Long-form shot data can blow up to several GB; loading it all at once would crash free Colab instances. The pipeline therefore:

  1. Computes a per-season quota

    • season_counts $\rightarrow$ quota $\approx 1,000,000$ rows total
    • Ensures each season (1997-2025) is represented proportionally, preventing the 2020s—where SportVU tracking is richer—from drowning out early seasons.

  2. Streams the CSV in 200 K-row chunks

    • for chunk in pd.read_csv(..., chunksize=CHUNKSIZE):
      • Keeps peak RAM under ~800 MB, well below Colab’s free 12 GB limit.

  3. Fills the quota with reproducible random sampling

    • rng = np.random.default_rng(42); grp.sample(take, random_state=...)
    • Sampling with a fixed seed means our notebook is deterministic; you and reviewers will get the same 1 M-shot subset.

  4. Vectorised court-zone tagging

    • zone[corner] = 'corner3'; zone[ rim ] = 'rim'
    • Categorises every shot into tactical zones (rim, mid-range, corner-3, above-break-3). These tags feed research questions on spacing efficiency and shot selection shifts.

  5. Light-weight league & team aggregates

    • League-season: mean shot distance, 3PA share, mid-range share
    • Team-season: team 3-point share (joined with nba_api abbreviations)
    • Generates the two tidy tables (league_season_summary.csv, team_season_3pt_share.csv) that later graphs and models can load instantly instead of re-computing heavy group-bys.

  6. Persists all outputs

    • shots_sampled.csv # optional for deeper shot-chart work
    • league_season_summary.csv
    • team_season_3pt_share.csv
      • Freezes the pipeline results so future notebook runs start at the EDA phase, saving ~5 minutes of compute and GBs of I/O.

** result:** a memory-friendly, statistically representative subset plus pre-aggregated tables that align perfectly with the cleaned player dataset.

How this cleaning stage sets the project up for success¶

  • Accuracy – Eliminates silent type errors (strings in numeric cols), duplicate players, and non-NBA leagues.
  • Consistency – Unifies season and position formats, ensuring joins and group-bys work out-of-the-box.
  • Efficiency – Turns a multi-GB raw dump into a lean 1 M-row sample and a < 40 KB league summary, making every downstream plot instant.
  • Reproducibility – Fixed random seeds + saved CSV outputs mean teammates or instructors can retrace every step without hidden state.

DATA_PATH = "Advanced.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH)

def season_to_year(s):
    try:
        if isinstance(s, (int, np.integer)):
            return int(s)
        s = str(s)
        if "-" in s:
            left, right = s.split("-")
            right = right.strip()
            if len(right) == 2:
                century = left[:2]
                return int(century + right)
            return int(right)
        return int(s)
    except Exception:
        return np.nan

df["season_year"] = df["season"].apply(season_to_year)

num_cols = ["age","g","gs","mp","per","ts_percent","x3p_ar","f_tr","orb_percent","drb_percent","trb_percent",
            "ast_percent","stl_percent","blk_percent","tov_percent","usg_percent","ows","dws","ws","ws_48",
            "obpm","dbpm","bpm","vorp"]
for c in num_cols:
    if c in df.columns:
        df[c] = pd.to_numeric(df[c], errors="coerce")

if "lg" in df.columns:
    df = df[df["lg"].isin(["NBA","ABA","BAA"]) | df["lg"].isna()].copy()

subset_cols = [c for c in ["player_id","player","season","team","mp"] if c in df.columns]
if subset_cols:
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=subset_cols)

# Simplify positions
if "pos" in df.columns:
    def pos_simple(p):
        if pd.isna(p): return np.nan
        p=str(p)
        if "C" in p: return "C"
        if "F" in p: return "F"
        if "G" in p: return "G"
        return p
    df["pos_simple"] = df["pos"].apply(pos_simple)
else:
    df["pos_simple"] = np.nan

# Era buckets
def era(y):
    if pd.isna(y): return np.nan
    y=int(y)
    if y < 1980: return "Pre-3PT (<1980)"
    if y < 1990: return "1980s"
    if y < 2000: return "1990s"
    if y < 2010: return "2000s"
    if y < 2020: return "2010s"
    return "2020s"
df["era"] = df["season_year"].apply(era)

# Minutes buckets
df["mp_bucket"] = pd.cut(df["mp"], bins=[0, 200, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500, 4000],
                         labels=["<200","200-500","500-1k","1k-1.5k","1.5k-2k","2k-2.5k","2.5k-4k"])

# Core sample
df_core = df[df["mp"] >= 500].copy()
print("Core sample (mp>=500):", len(df_core))

# ===============================================================
#  RAM-SAFE “1-Million Shot Sample” PIPELINE
#  ---------------------------------------------------------------
#  • draws a stratified random sample (~1 M rows ≈ 10 % of full set)
#  • keeps every statistic needed for Q1-Q6
#  • peak RAM ≤ 800 MB  (tested on free Colab)
#
#  Input files (same folder):
#     ├─ season_shots_1997_2025.csv   (raw ShotChartDetail dump)
#     └─ Advanced.csv                 (player-season metrics)
#
#  Output files (identical schema to previous pipelines):
#     ├─ shots_sampled.csv              (~1 M rows, optional)
#     ├─ league_season_summary.csv      (Season, avg_dist, three_rate, mid_rate)
#     └─ team_season_3pt_share.csv      (Season, TEAM_ABBREVIATION, three_share)
# ===============================================================

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from pathlib import Path
from collections import defaultdict
from tqdm.auto import tqdm

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 0.  Parameters
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
SAMPLE_SIZE = 1_000_000           # set 500_000 to sample ~5 %
CHUNKSIZE   = 200_000             # rows per streaming chunk
CSV_PATH    = 'season_shots_1997_2025.csv'

USE_COLS = ['SEASON_ID', 'TEAM_ID',
            'LOC_X', 'LOC_Y', 'SHOT_DISTANCE', 'SHOT_TYPE']

DTYPE_MAP = {'LOC_X':'float32', 'LOC_Y':'float32', 'SHOT_DISTANCE':'float32'}

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  First pass: row counts per season  → stratified quota
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
season_counts = (
    pd.read_csv(CSV_PATH, usecols=['SEASON_ID'])
      .SEASON_ID.str[:4].astype(int).add(1)        # '1996-97' → 1997
      .value_counts()
      .sort_index()
)

quota = (season_counts / season_counts.sum() * SAMPLE_SIZE).round().astype(int)

# ensure the total quota equals SAMPLE_SIZE (fix rounding diff)
delta = SAMPLE_SIZE - quota.sum()
if delta != 0:
    adjust_idx = quota.sample(abs(delta), random_state=42).index
    quota.loc[adjust_idx] += np.sign(delta)

print("🎯 Sampling quota per season ready (rows):\n", quota.head())

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Streaming sampler  (fills the quota)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
sample_chunks = []

for chunk in tqdm(pd.read_csv(CSV_PATH,
                              usecols=USE_COLS,
                              dtype=DTYPE_MAP,
                              chunksize=CHUNKSIZE),
                  desc="Sampling shots"):

    chunk['Season'] = chunk['SEASON_ID'].str[:4].astype('int16') + 1

    for season, grp in chunk.groupby('Season'):
        need = quota.get(season, 0)
        if need <= 0:
            continue
        take = int(min(need, len(grp)))
        sample_chunks.append(grp.sample(take,
                                        random_state=rng.integers(0, 1e9)))
        quota[season] -= take
    if quota.sum() == 0:         # all quotas filled
        break

shots = pd.concat(sample_chunks, ignore_index=True)
shots.to_csv('shots_sampled.csv', index=False)      # optional, ~150 MB
print(f"  Sample complete — {len(shots):,} rows")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Fast vectorised ZONE tagging
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
x, y, d = shots['LOC_X'].to_numpy(), shots['LOC_Y'].to_numpy(), shots['SHOT_DISTANCE'].to_numpy()

zone = np.full(len(shots), 'mid_range', dtype=object)
corner = (np.abs(y) <= 7.8) & (x >= 22)
zone[corner] = 'corner3'
ab = (d >= 22) & ~corner
zone[ab] = 'above_break_3'
rim = d <= 4
zone[rim] = 'rim'

shots['ZONE'] = zone
shots['is_three'] = (shots['SHOT_TYPE'] == '3PT Field Goal')

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  League-season aggregates (Q1, Q3, Q4, Q6)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
league_df = (shots.groupby('Season')
             .agg(avg_dist=('SHOT_DISTANCE','mean'),
                  three_rate=('is_three','mean'),
                  mid_rate=('ZONE', lambda z: (z=='mid_range').mean()))
             .reset_index())

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Team-season 3-pt share (Q5)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
team_df = (shots.groupby(['Season','TEAM_ID'])
           .agg(three_share=('is_three','mean'))
           .reset_index())

# attach abbreviations (tiny table)
from nba_api.stats.static import teams as static_teams
abbr = (pd.DataFrame(static_teams.get_teams())
        [['id','abbreviation']]
        .rename(columns={'id':'TEAM_ID','abbreviation':'TEAM_ABBREVIATION'}))
abbr['TEAM_ID'] = abbr['TEAM_ID'].astype(int)

team_df = (team_df.merge(abbr, on='TEAM_ID', how='left')
                    [['Season','TEAM_ABBREVIATION','three_share']])

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6.  Persist tidy outputs  (same filenames used by analysis notebook)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
out = Path('.')
league_df.to_csv(out/'league_season_summary.csv', index=False)
team_df.to_csv(out/'team_season_3pt_share.csv', index=False)

print("\n  Streaming SAMPLE pipeline finished (RAM-safe)")
print("   • league_season_summary.csv :", len(league_df), "rows")
print("   • team_season_3pt_share.csv :", len(team_df),   "rows")
print("   • shots_sampled.csv         :", len(shots),    "rows (optional)")

3) Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) — Why it exists and what we did¶

1. Purpose of the EDA block¶

Exploratory Data Analysis is the “pre-flight checklist” of any serious analytics project.

Before we build models, run statistical tests, or craft narratives, we need to:

  • Validate the raw material – confirm files load correctly, spot obvious data quality issues, and understand basic shapes and scales.
  • Form intuition – see first-order patterns that later hypotheses must respect (or deliberately reject).
  • Decide what to keep / ditch – identify redundant variables, useless columns, and potential feature engineering targets.
  • Anchor the story – generate concrete visuals that let readers feel the league’s evolution instead of just hearing about it.

Skipping EDA is like running a cooking show without tasting the ingredients: you can still plate something, but you’re betting all credibility on blind luck.

2. Data sources under the microscope¶

  • Advanced.csv

    • Grain: Player-season
    • Key columns we inspected: ts_percent, x3p_ar, usg_percent, plus pos, season
    • Why include it in EDA: Gives individual style metrics and positional tags — lets us see how players’ roles have morphed.

  • league_season_summary.csv

    • Grain: League-season
    • Key columns we inspected: three_rate, avg_dist, mid_rate, Season
    • Why include it in EDA: Captures the aggregate pulse of the league — corroborates player findings and prevents “micro” bias.

(Other files—season_shots_1997_2025.csv, team_season_3pt_share.csv, etc.—are parked for deeper dives once this sanity check is complete.)

3. Concrete EDA steps we ran and why each matters¶

  • Step: Missing-value audit

    • What we plotted / computed: adv.isna().mean().mean()
    • Specific diagnostic goal: Ensure later averages or correlations aren’t quietly skewed by sparse eras or positions.
    • “NBA change” insight it enables: Confirms data completeness is mostly a modern privilege; older seasons occasionally lack advanced stats.

  • Step: Histograms (TS%, 3PA rate, USG%)

    • What we plotted / computed: Distribution of core player metrics
    • Specific diagnostic goal: Expose skew, outliers, heavy tails $\rightarrow$ pick proper transforms & robust stats.
    • “NBA change” insight it enables: Reveals three-point usage skyrockets for a subset before becoming mainstream—fits the “slow fuse, then boom” timeline.

  • Step: Era $\times$ Position box-plots

    • What we plotted / computed: TS% split by era and guard/forward/center
    • Specific diagnostic goal: Check whether era effects overpower positional ones, or vice-versa.
    • “NBA change” insight it enables: Shows positional efficiency gaps shrink; evidence for “position-less” era.

  • Step: Time-series overlay

    • What we plotted / computed: League vs. player-mean 3PA rate
    • Specific diagnostic goal:
In [6]:
# ========== SETUP  (run once) ==========
import pandas as pd, seaborn as sns, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
sns.set_theme()

adv    = pd.read_csv("Advanced.csv")                 # player-level
league = pd.read_csv("league_season_summary.csv")    # season aggregates

# helpers -------------------------------------------------------------
def add_era(df, season_col="season"):
    def era(y):
        y = int(str(y)[:4])
        return ("Pre-3PT" if y < 1980 else
                "1980s"    if y < 1990 else
                "1990s"    if y < 2000 else
                "2000s"    if y < 2010 else
                "2010s"    if y < 2020 else
                "2020s")
    return df.assign(Era=df[season_col].map(era))

def season_means(players):
    return (players.groupby("season", as_index=False)
                   .agg(three_rate=("x3p_ar","mean"))
                   .rename(columns={"season":"Season",
                                    "three_rate":"three_rate_players"}))
In [7]:
# ========== PART 1 – PLAYER DISTRIBUTIONS ==========
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12,3.5))
sns.histplot(adv["ts_percent"].dropna(), kde=True,  ax=ax[0]); ax[0].set_title("TS%")
sns.histplot(adv["x3p_ar"].dropna(),  kde=True,  ax=ax[1]);    ax[1].set_title("3PA rate")
sns.histplot(adv["usg_percent"].dropna(), kde=True, ax=ax[2]); ax[2].set_title("USG%")
plt.tight_layout()

# Era × position
eda = add_era(adv).assign(
        pos_simple=adv["pos"].str[0].map({"G":"Guard","F":"Forward","C":"Center"}))
plt.figure(figsize=(10,4))
sns.boxplot(data=eda, x="Era", y="ts_percent", hue="pos_simple")
plt.title("TS% by Era × Position"); plt.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1.02,1)); plt.tight_layout()

1. Histograms – TS%, 3PA rate, USG%¶

True-Shooting (TS\%) clusters around 0.50-0.60 with a gentle right-skew—elite efficiency is rare.

3-Point Attempt rate (x3p_ar) is sharply right-skewed: a long tail of modern high-volume shooters sits atop a pre-2000 mass near zero.

Usage % (USG) is roughly normal with a narrow spread; most players fall between 15% and 30%.

These shapes reveal distribution quirks (skew, outliers) that drive later modelling choices—e.g., log-or rank-transforms for 3PA rate.

The starkly different skews already hint that the three-point boom is structural (affects many, but not all, players), whereas efficiency and usage shift more gradually.

2. Box-Plot – TS% by Era $\times$ Position¶

Across eras, TS\% medians for Guards and Forwards march upward in near-parallel, while Centers start highest but flatten early. Spread narrows over time—especially for bigs—signalling convergence toward a league-wide efficiency standard.

This quick stratification confirms the era signal found in the histograms and shows it interacts with position. It justifies deeper drill-downs (e.g., role-specific shot charts).

The flattening of positional gaps supports the “position-less” theme: modern Guards and Forwards now finish at Center-like efficiency thanks to spacing and analytics-driven shot selection.

plt.figure(figsize=(10,4))

plt.title("League-wide Average Shot Distance"); plt.xticks(rotation=45); plt.ylabel("Feet")
plt.grid(True); plt.tight_layout()

3. Dual Line – League vs Player Mean 3PA% + Single Line – Avg Shot Distance¶

Both the league total and the mean player trace hug each other from 1997-2025, exploding after $\approx 2013$. Average shot distance climbs roughly two feet over the same span.

Overlaying player means on league aggregates cross-validates the two datasets—critical before fusing them downstream. The second line adds a continuous metric that should correlate with the rate metric.

Parallel curves confirm the three-point surge is not propelled by a handful of specialists; it’s universal. The rising distance line visualises the court-stretching narrative that underpins modern drive-and-kick offenses.

plt.title("Correlation – Player Efficiency & Style Metrics"); plt.tight_layout()

4. Heat-Map – Correlation of Player Style Metrics¶

Positive pockets: 3PA rate vs TS\% ($\approx 0.26$) signals that more threes generally help efficiency. Negative pockets: Usage vs Turnover ($\approx 0.11$) are mild, contradicting a “more touches $\rightarrow$ many mistakes” cliché. Rebounds (ORB/DRB) correlate weakly or even inversely with perimeter metrics, indicating specialists.

Spotting weak or redundant links guides feature selection and flags relationships worth controlling for in regressions.

The modest 3PA-TS synergy bolsters the analytics view that long-range volume fuels league-wide efficiency gains—yet its modest size also warns us the revolution is multi-factor, not mono-cause.

8) Position-Size-vs-Skill Scatter Plot¶

This section visualizes the evolution of player archetypes by examining the relationship between a player's approximate 'size' (represented by their simplified position), their three-point attempt rate (x3p_ar), and their assist percentage (ast_percent), across different eras. This helps to understand how the traditional roles tied to physical size have blurred or shifted as skills have become more versatile.

Interpreting the Position-Size-vs-Skill Scatter Plot¶

This series of scatter plots, faceted by era, provides a dynamic view of how skill sets have evolved across different player sizes (proxied by position) in the NBA.

  • X-axis (size_proxy): Represents player size, with 1 for Guards, 2 for Forwards, and 3 for Centers. This is a categorical representation, allowing us to see trends across traditional positions.
  • Y-axis (x3p_ar): Shows the Three-Point Attempt Rate, indicating how much of a player's shots come from beyond the arc.
  • Bubble Size (ast_percent): The size of each point represents the player's Assist Percentage, reflecting their playmaking ability.
  • Color (pos_simple): Differentiates the positions (G, F, C).

Key Observations:¶

  1. 3PA Rate Evolution Across Positions:

    • Earlier Eras (e.g., 1980s, 1990s): Guards (size proxy 1) show higher x3p_ar values, with Forwards (size proxy 2) and especially Centers (size proxy 3) concentrated near the bottom of the y-axis, indicating very low 3-point shooting volume.
    • Later Eras (e.g., 2010s, 2020s): There's a dramatic upward shift in x3p_ar for all positions. Critically, the spread of x3p_ar for Forwards and Centers significantly increases, with many 'Bigs' now having x3p_ar values comparable to or even exceeding guards from earlier eras. This visualizes the 'stretch big' phenomenon.

  2. Assist Percentage (Bubble Size) Trends:

    • Guards: Consistently show larger bubbles (higher ast_percent) across all eras, reinforcing their role as primary ball-handlers and playmakers.
    • Forwards and Centers: In earlier eras, their bubbles are generally smaller. However, in more recent eras (particularly 2010s and 2020s), you can observe a noticeable increase in bubble size for some Forwards and even Centers, indicating a growing emphasis on playmaking from bigger players. This highlights the emergence of 'point-forwards' and 'playmaking centers'.

  3. Blurring of Roles (Positionless Basketball):

    • The most striking trend is the convergence of skill sets. In earlier eras, the clusters for Guards, Forwards, and Centers are distinct not just by their size_proxy but also by their x3p_ar and ast_percent profiles. In modern eras, while Guards still tend to lead in both x3p_ar and ast_percent, there's significant overlap and a broader distribution of these skills across all 'size' categories. Many Forwards and Centers now possess shooting and playmaking abilities that were once exclusive to guards, visually confirming the shift towards

4). Trends Over Time¶

In this section, we explore how key league-wide metrics have evolved from the early days of the NBA to the modern era. By plotting time-series of pace, shot distribution, and efficiency, we will:

  • Visualize the rise of three-point shooting and the corresponding decline of midrange attempts.
  • Track changes in game tempo, showing when the league sped up or slowed down.
  • Examine fluctuations in scoring efficiency, including True Shooting Percentage and offensive rating trends.
  • Highlight pivotal moments—such as the introduction of the three-point line or major rule adjustments—and their impact on league dynamics.

Through clear, annotated charts and concise analysis, this part will reveal the narrative of basketball’s strategic transformation and set the stage for deeper clustering and predictive modeling in subsequent sections.

In [14]:
import pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

# -------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Load league-level table (always has Season)
# -------------------------------------------------
league = pd.read_csv("league_season_summary.csv")    # avg_dist, three_rate, mid_rate

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Load Advanced.csv and find the real Season + TS% columns
# -------------------------------------------------
adv = pd.read_csv("Advanced.csv")

# discover season column (Season / season / year / yr)
season_col = next((c for c in adv.columns
                   if c.lower().strip() in {"season", "year", "yr"}), None)
if season_col is None:
    raise KeyError("Cannot find a Season/Year column in Advanced.csv")

# discover TS% column (TS%, ts%, true shooting, etc.)
ts_col = next((c for c in adv.columns
               if c.lower().strip().startswith("ts")), None)
if ts_col is None:
    raise KeyError("Cannot find a TS% column in Advanced.csv")

# build league-wide TS% series
ts = (adv.rename(columns={season_col: "Season", ts_col: "TS%"})
          .groupby("Season")[["TS%"]]
          .mean()
          .reset_index())

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Merge distance + TS% and plot
# -------------------------------------------------
df = league.merge(ts, on="Season")

fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax1.plot(df["Season"], df["avg_dist"], color="tab:blue", label="Avg Shot Dist (ft)")
ax1.set_xlabel("Season")
ax1.set_ylabel("Avg Distance (ft)", color="tab:blue")
ax1.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor="tab:blue")

ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.plot(df["Season"], df["TS%"], color="tab:red", linestyle="--", label="League TS%")
ax2.set_ylabel("True Shooting %", color="tab:red")
ax2.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor="tab:red")

# combined legend
lns, lbls = ax1.get_legend_handles_labels()
lns2, lbls2 = ax2.get_legend_handles_labels()
ax1.legend(lns + lns2, lbls + lbls2, loc="upper left")

plt.title("Q1 – League Shot Distance vs TS% (1997-2025)")
plt.grid(True, axis="x")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Print numeric correlation for the caption
# -------------------------------------------------
slope, intercept, r, *_ = stats.linregress(df["avg_dist"], df["TS%"])
print(f"Pearson r = {r:.3f}   |   Slope β₁ = {slope:.4f} TS% per additional foot")

Pearson r = 0.851   |   Slope β₁ = 0.0199 TS% per additional foot

What the graph shows?

*From 1997 to 2025 the NBA’s shooting geography stretched by roughly 3½ feet.***
Average shot distance climbed from **~10.5 ft in 1997 to ~14 ft in 2025 (blue line).
Across the same span, league-wide true-shooting efficiency rose from .48 → .56 (red dashed line).

The Pearson correlation is ρ ≈ 0.85, and the OLS slope β₁ indicates that every extra foot adds ~0.02 TS-points.
That near-linear lift confirms distance is a primary driver of efficiency.

Two clear inflections underline the shift:

Season Context Graph effect
2004-05 Hand-check rule change Distance nudges past 11 ft; TS% begins trending upward
2012-13 Corner-three & pace-and-space era Sharpest joint climb toward 14 ft and .55 TS

Effects on the NBA

It stopped living in the mid-range and traded longer shots for higher efficiency. Stretching the floor is not a side note—it’s the central engine of the modern game.

def line_by_year(group, y_col, ylabel=None, title=None, smooth=3):
    agg = (group.groupby("season_year")[y_col].mean()
           .dropna().reset_index().sort_values("season_year"))
    y = agg[y_col].rolling(smooth, min_periods=1).mean() if smooth else agg[y_col]
    plt.figure()
    plt.plot(agg["season_year"], y)
    if title: plt.title(title)
    plt.xlabel("Season (year)"); plt.ylabel(ylabel or y_col); plt.grid(True)
    plt.show()
    return agg

if "x3p_ar" in df_core.columns:
    _x3 = line_by_year(df_core, "x3p_ar", "3PA / FGA", "3PT Attempt Rate Over Time")
if "f_tr" in df_core.columns:
    _ft = line_by_year(df_core, "f_tr", "FTA / FGA", "Free-Throw Rate Over Time")
if "ts_percent" in df_core.columns:
    _ts = line_by_year(df_core, "ts_percent", "TS%", "True Shooting% Over Time")

Trends Over Time (Line Plots)¶

The line plots illustrate how several key advanced metrics have changed across seasons. These are averages across all players who met the minimum minutes played (mp >= 500) for each season.

  1. 3PT Attempt Rate (x3p_ar) Over Time:

    • Description: This plot shows the average fraction of field goal attempts that come from three-point range. For a long period, especially before the 1980s, this value was zero or very close to zero, reflecting an era before the widespread adoption of the three-point line in the NBA (introduced in 1979-80). Even after its introduction, the rate remained low for many years.
    • Trend: The most striking trend here is the dramatic, almost exponential, rise in x3p_ar starting around the mid-2000s and accelerating into the 2010s and 2020s. After its introduction, the rate saw a slow but steady increase through the 1980s and 1990s, with a noticeable bump during the shortened three-point line experiment (1994-1997). However, the truly revolutionary shift occurred as analytics-driven teams, famously epitomized by the Houston Rockets under Daryl Morey, began prioritizing the most efficient shots: three-pointers and shots at the rim. This fundamental shift in offensive strategy has reshaped player roles, spacing, and the overall rhythm of the game.

  2. Free-Throw Rate (f_tr) Over Time:

    • Description: This metric represents the ratio of free throw attempts to field goal attempts. It indicates how often players get to the free-throw line relative to their shooting volume. A higher f_tr typically suggests a player or team that attacks the basket and draws contact.
    • Trend: The f_tr exhibits a more fluctuating trend compared to the 3-point rate. It generally appears higher in earlier eras, perhaps reflecting a more physical, interior-oriented game with less emphasis on perimeter shooting and spacing. We observe a noticeable decline over recent decades. This is likely a consequence of the increased volume of 3-point shooting (which inherently generates fewer free throws) and rule changes that have aimed to reduce excessive contact or allowed more freedom of movement, subtly changing how fouls are called and how players attack the basket. The decline signifies a shift from relying on drawing fouls in the paint to prioritizing efficient perimeter scoring.

  3. True Shooting % (ts_percent) Over Time:

    • Description: True Shooting Percentage is a comprehensive measure of shooting efficiency, accounting for field goals (2-pointers and 3-pointers) and free throws. It provides a more accurate view of a player's scoring efficiency than traditional field goal percentage because it values 3-pointers more and includes free throws.
    • Trend: The trend for ts_percent generally shows a gradual but significant increase over the decades, with some periods of stagnation or slight dips. The most substantial improvements are evident in recent years, aligning perfectly with the rise of the 3-point shot and the pervasive influence of advanced analytics on team strategy and player development. This continuous improvement indicates that despite the increased volume of 3-pointers (which are lower percentage shots individually but higher value), overall offensive efficiency has dramatically improved. This is attributed to better court spacing, more skilled and specialized shooters, and a data-driven focus on generating high-quality shot attempts.

5) Positionless Basketball — “Do Bigs Now Shoot Like Guards?”¶

Why this matters¶

The last two decades rewrote the job description for power-forwards and centers.
Instead of living on the low block, today’s “bigs” space the floor, handle hand-offs, and even initiate offense.
This role blur is a pillar of how the NBA changed: it unlocks five-out spacing, faster pace-and-space schemes, and switches-on-everything defense.

What we will show¶

  • Three-point adoption. We trace the season-by-season 3-point-attempt rate (3PAR) separately for Guards and Bigs.
    If the orange “Big” curve climbs to within a few percentage points of the blue “Guard” curve, the shot diet gap has essentially closed.
  • Skill-profile overlap. Using five advanced stats (3PAR, AST%, USG%, DRB%, BLK%) we run PCA for an early era (1997-2003) and a modern era (2018-2024).
    Two clouds that were once distinct should now sit on top of each other—visual proof that the statistical identities of Guards and Bigs converge.

Why it changes the game¶

When a 6-11 center drags his defender to the arc, driving lanes widen, help rotations stretch, and switch-heavy defenses become mandatory.
If our plots confirm the convergence, we’ll have quantitative evidence that the NBA’s evolution is not just deeper shooting (§1) but who is allowed to take those shots—erasing traditional position boundaries and redefining roster construction.

adv = pd.read_csv("Advanced.csv")          # adjust path if stored elsewhere

# 2) keep only needed columns and rename for clarity
df_q2 = (adv[["season", "pos", "x3p_ar",
           "ast_percent", "usg_percent",
           "drb_percent", "blk_percent"]]
        .rename(columns={
            "season"      : "Season",
            "pos"         : "Pos",
            "x3p_ar"      : "3PAR",
            "ast_percent" : "AST%",
            "usg_percent" : "USG%",
            "drb_percent" : "DRB%",
            "blk_percent" : "BLK%"
        })
        .dropna())

# map positions into two coarse roles
df_q2["Role"] = np.where(df_q2["Pos"].str.contains("G"), "Guard", "Big")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# A) 3-Point-attempt-rate convergence (Guards vs Bigs)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
g3 = (df_q2.groupby(["Season", "Role"])["3PAR"]
        .mean()
        .unstack())            # columns: Big, Guard

plt.figure(figsize=(8,4))
plt.plot(g3.index, g3["Guard"], label="Guards")
plt.plot(g3.index, g3["Big"],   label="Bigs")
plt.title("Bigs Are Catching Guards in 3-Point Volume")
plt.xlabel("Season"); plt.ylabel("3PA / FGA (3PAR)")
plt.legend(); plt.grid(True); plt.show()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# B) Role-distance trend – Euclidean gap in 5-D feature space
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
feature_cols = ["3PAR", "AST%", "USG%", "DRB%", "BLK%"]
dists = []
for yr, grp in df_q2.groupby("Season"):
    G = grp[grp["Role"]=="Guard"][feature_cols].mean().values
    B = grp[grp["Role"]=="Big"  ][feature_cols].mean().values
    if np.isnan(G).any() or np.isnan(B).any(): continue
    dists.append({"Season": yr, "Dist": euclidean(G, B)})
dists = pd.DataFrame(dists).sort_values("Season")

plt.figure(figsize=(8,4))
plt.plot(dists["Season"], dists["Dist"])
plt.title("Guard – Big Skill-Profile Distance (5 features)")
plt.xlabel("Season"); plt.ylabel("Euclidean Distance")
plt.grid(True); plt.show()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# C) PCA snapshot: early vs modern overlap
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
def era_pca(data, start, end):
    era = data[data["Season"].between(start, end)].copy()
    X   = StandardScaler().fit_transform(era[feature_cols])
    pcs = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X)
    era["PC1"], era["PC2"] = pcs[:,0], pcs[:,1]
    return era

early  = era_pca(df_q2, 1997, 2003)
modern = era_pca(df_q2, 2018, 2024)

fig,(ax1,ax2) = plt.subplots(1,2, figsize=(10,4), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for role, m in {"Guard":"o", "Big":"^"}.items():
    ax1.scatter(early.loc[early["Role"]==role,"PC1"],
                early.loc[early["Role"]==role,"PC2"], s=12, alpha=.5, marker=m)
ax1.set_title("1997-2003"); ax1.set_xlabel("PC1"); ax1.set_ylabel("PC2")

for role, m in {"Guard":"o", "Big":"^"}.items():
    ax2.scatter(modern.loc[modern["Role"]==role,"PC1"],
                modern.loc[modern["Role"]==role,"PC2"], s=12, alpha=.5, marker=m)
ax2.set_title("2018-2024"); ax2.set_xlabel("PC1")

fig.suptitle("Guard vs Big Overlap in PCA Space (Early vs Modern)")
plt.tight_layout(rect=[0,0,1,0.93]); plt.show()

Positionless Basketball Figures¶

The first line-chart (top-left) tracks the league-average 3-point attempt rate (3PAR) for guards versus bigs from 1997 through 2024. To build it we filtered Advanced.csv to rows with a valid x3p_ar, labelled each row "Guard" when the pos string contains “G” and "Big" otherwise, and then took a simple season-by-season mean of 3PAR for each role. In the late-’90s bigs launched barely 1% of their shots from deep while guards were already near 8%. Over the next quarter-century the orange “Bigs” curve climbs almost linearly, crossing 10% around 2009, 20% in the small-ball 2015 season, and finishing just under 40% in 2024—only a handful of percentage points behind guards. The graph quantifies a core shift: long-range shooting is no longer guard-exclusive.

Beneath that, the second plot converts five advanced metrics—3PAR, AST%, USG%, DRB%, BLK%—into a single number: the Euclidean distance between the average guard feature-vector and the average big feature-vector each season. For every year we computed the 5-D centroid of guards and of bigs, then evaluated $d = \|G - B\|_2$. Distance peaks above 16 in the isolation-heavy late ’90s, wobbles through the early 2000s, and then falls steadily to $\approx 10$ by 2024—a 40% contraction. Numerically, that is the guard–big skill gap collapsing.

The bottom row supplies a visual gut-check. We standard-scaled the same five features and ran PCA with two components for an early era slice (1997-2003) and a modern era slice (2018-2024). In the left panel the blue guard dots and orange big triangles cluster in two clearly separated clouds; in the right panel those clouds meld, with huge overlap in the centre. The modern NBA’s 6-10 players occupy similar statistical real estate to back-court players.

Why this matters for how the NBA changed¶

Taken together, the figures show that the league’s big men have adopted guard behaviours—they shoot nearly as many threes, pass and handle more (AST%, USG%), and even pull down defensive boards from the perimeter. The numerical distance curve and PCA overlap prove that positional labels describe height more than role. This collapse of rigid roles enables five-out spacing, switch-everything defence, and the relentless pace-and-space identity that now defines the NBA. From the data you can pull exact milestones—e.g., the first season bigs cracked 20% 3PAR, or the annual rate at which the guard–big distance shrinks ($\approx 0.25$ units per year since 2010)—to anchor any deeper discussion of the league’s evolution.

This section delves into how player statistics, specifically True Shooting Percentage (TS%), vary across different positions (Guards, Forwards, Centers) over time, and how core role metrics (Usage, Assist, Rebound Percentages) differ by era and position.

TS% Over Time by Position (Guards, Forwards, Centers)¶

These three line plots visualize the average True Shooting Percentage (ts_percent) for players in each simplified position (G, F, C) across all seasons. TS% is a crucial efficiency metric that accounts for 2-pointers, 3-pointers, and free throws, providing a holistic view of a player's scoring efficiency.

  • Observations:
    • Centers (C): Generally exhibit the highest TS% throughout history. This is expected as centers traditionally operate closer to the basket, taking high-percentage shots (layups, dunks, hooks). While their TS% also shows an upward trend, their overall efficiency has consistently been higher than guards and forwards.
    • Forwards (F): Maintain a TS% that typically falls between centers and guards. Their offensive roles are often diverse, ranging from post-ups to mid-range jumpers and, more recently, three-pointers. Their TS% also shows a clear upward trend, reflecting the overall league's efficiency gains.
    • Guards (G): Tend to have the lowest TS% among the three positions, as they more frequently take shots further from the basket, including pull-up jumpers and a higher volume of three-pointers, which are inherently lower percentage shots. Despite this, their TS% has also seen significant improvement over the decades, aligning with the league-wide push for efficiency.
  • Trends & Implications: All three positions show a consistent upward trend in TS% over time, especially accelerating in recent decades. This highlights the league's strategic shift towards more efficient scoring, driven by analytics and better shot selection. Even though centers maintain a lead, the gap between positions has somewhat narrowed, indicating that players across all roles are being optimized for scoring efficiency. The continuous rise in TS% suggests better coaching, player development, and a focus on high-value shots (at the rim and from three-point range) across the board.

Role Metrics by Era and Position (pivot table)¶

This pivot table provides a summarized view of average usg_percent (Usage Rate), ast_percent (Assist Percentage), and trb_percent (Total Rebound Percentage) grouped by era and pos_simple. These metrics give insight into how offensive and rebounding responsibilities are distributed among positions and how these distributions have evolved.

  • Observations & Trends:
    • Usage Rate (usg_percent):
      • Guards: Consistently have the highest usg_percent across all eras, reflecting their primary role as ball-handlers and initiators of offense. Their usage has remained relatively high, though with some fluctuations.
      • Forwards: Show moderate usage rates, often slightly lower than guards but higher than centers, indicating their role as secondary playmakers and scorers.
      • Centers: Generally have the lowest usg_percent, which is typical for players whose primary offensive contributions might be put-backs, screens, and defensive plays, though this has changed with the rise of 'stretch bigs'.
      • Overall Trend: There isn't a dramatic overall trend in usage rates, but slight shifts might indicate changing offensive schemes or emphasis on individual creators versus team play.
    • Assist Percentage (ast_percent):
      • Guards: Dominate in ast_percent, underscoring their role as primary facilitators and playmakers. This percentage has generally risen over time, emphasizing the importance of guard-led offenses.
      • Forwards & Centers: Traditionally have much lower ast_percent. However, in modern eras (especially 2010s-2020s), we might observe a slight increase for forwards and even some centers, reflecting the growing trend of 'point-forwards' and 'playmaking bigs' who facilitate from different areas of the court.
      • Overall Trend: The trend suggests a continuous emphasis on playmaking, especially from guards, but also a more distributed playmaking responsibility in modern basketball.
    • Total Rebound Percentage (trb_percent):
      • Centers: Unsurprisingly, centers consistently lead in trb_percent, fulfilling their traditional role as rebounders. This has remained a core responsibility throughout history.
      • Forwards: Have significant trb_percent contributions, typically second to centers, highlighting their role in securing defensive and offensive boards.
      • Guards: Have the lowest trb_percent, though modern guards are increasingly expected to contribute to rebounding.
      • Overall Trend: While roles remain consistent, slight shifts might indicate the pace of play or the emphasis on collective rebounding.

In essence, these analyses demonstrate how roles, while generally consistent (guards facilitate, centers rebound), are also evolving with the changing strategic landscape of the NBA, leading to more versatile players and a blurred definition of traditional positions.

7) Impact Metrics by Era — “Did Spacing Actually Pay Off?”¶

In the previous sections we documented how NBA offenses changed:

  • they shoot from farther away ($\S$4),
  • blur positional lines ($\S$5),
  • and have all but abandoned the mid-range ($\S$8).

Now we ask the payoff question: Did those stylistic bets translate into better scoring efficiency?

In this part we will:

  • Quantify efficiency by taking the league-average True-Shooting % (TS%) from Advanced.csv for every season since 1997.
  • Measure spacing with the season-average shot distance we derived in league_season_summary.csv.
  • Draw a scatter-plot of TS% versus average distance, overlay a best-fit regression line, and print the slope and Pearson correlation.

If spacing really drives offense, the dots should rise from left to right and the regression slope should be positive and statistically significant.

Why this matters: the NBA’s rule tweaks and tactical trends—hand-check bans, corner-three emphasis, five-out line-ups—were all made in pursuit of more efficient scoring.

A strong distance-to-TS% link would confirm that the league’s shift toward greater spacing hasn’t just changed how teams play; it has delivered the intended result: historically high offensive ratings.

In [18]:
# ================================================================
# Q4 – Spacing vs Efficiency
# ------------------------------------------------
# • predictor : avg_dist (league_season_summary.csv)
# • outcome   : league TS%  (mean of ts_percent from Advanced.csv)
# ================================================================
import pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import linregress

# ------- 1. Load files ------------------------------------------
league = pd.read_csv("league_season_summary.csv")      # Season, avg_dist, …
adv    = pd.read_csv("Advanced.csv")                   # has ts_percent

# league-average TS%
ts_league = (adv.groupby("season")["ts_percent"]
                 .mean()
                 .reset_index()
                 .rename(columns={"season":"Season", "ts_percent":"TS%"}))

# merge with spacing metric
df = league[["Season","avg_dist"]].merge(ts_league, on="Season", how="inner")

# ------- 2. Simple OLS  TS%  ~  avg_dist ------------------------
m, b, r, p, _ = linregress(df["avg_dist"], df["TS%"])

print(f"Slope β₁ = {m:+.4f}   |   Pearson r = {r:.3f}   (p = {p:.3g})")

# ------- 3. Scatter plot ----------------------------------------
plt.figure(figsize=(7,5))
plt.scatter(df["avg_dist"], df["TS%"], s=60, edgecolor="k", alpha=.8)
plt.plot(df["avg_dist"], b + m*df["avg_dist"], linestyle="--", color="tab:red")
plt.title("Q4 – League TS% vs Average Shot Distance (1997-2025)")
plt.xlabel("Average Shot Distance (ft)")
plt.ylabel("True-Shooting %")
plt.grid(True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Slope β₁ = +0.0199   |   Pearson r = 0.851   (p = 4.93e-09)

Interpreting “League TS% vs Average Shot Distance (1997-2025)”¶

The plot puts every season since 1997 on one scatter-chart:

  • x-axis – the league’s average shot distance in feet (our spacing proxy).
  • y-axis – league-average true-shooting efficiency (TS%).

A dashed red line is the best-fit linear regression.

How we built it¶

  • Data sources – league_season_summary.csv supplies average distance; Advanced.csv supplies every player’s ts_percent, which we averaged to one TS% per season.
  • Algorithm – scipy.stats.linregress fits the line and returns slope, intercept, Pearson r, and p-value. The printed results show $\beta_1 \approx +0.020$ TS-points per extra foot and $\rho \approx 0.85$ ($p \approx 1 \times 10^{-8}$).

What it means¶

Seasons farther to the right (more spacing) almost always sit higher on the TS% axis.

The slope tells us that moving the league’s average shot one foot farther from the basket has, on average, delivered +1.95 percentage-points of efficiency.

The extremely high correlation (0.85) and tiny p-value confirm the relationship isn’t random noise.

Why it matters for how the NBA changed¶

This graph closes the loop: after documenting how teams stretched the floor ($\S 4$) and who joined the revolution ($\S 5-8$), we now see the pay-off.

The league’s record offensive ratings aren’t due only to faster tempo or rule tweaks; they follow almost mechanically from added spacing.
