Correlation Heatmap¶

This heatmap visually represents the pairwise correlation coefficients between a selection of advanced statistics: ts_percent, x3p_ar, f_tr, usg_percent, ast_percent, trb_percent, tov_percent, bpm, vorp, per, and ws_48.

  • Key Observations and Trends:

    • Strong Positive Correlations with Overall Impact Metrics: Metrics like bpm (Box Plus/Minus), vorp (Value Over Replacement Player), per (Player Efficiency Rating), and ws_48 (Win Shares per 48 minutes) show strong positive correlations with each other (e.g., bpm and vorp have a correlation of 0.91, per and bpm at 0.85). This is expected, as these are all aggregate measures designed to capture a player's overall impact and productivity. A high value in one usually implies a high value in others.
    • TS% and Impact: ts_percent (True Shooting Percentage) shows moderately strong positive correlations with bpm (0.55), vorp (0.44), per (0.54), and ws_48 (0.68). This highlights the critical importance of offensive efficiency for overall player impact and team success. Players who score efficiently tend to contribute more to winning.
    • Usage vs. Efficiency: usg_percent (Usage Rate) has a moderate positive correlation with per (0.64) and bpm (0.40), suggesting that players with higher usage often have higher productivity. However, its correlation with ts_percent (0.07) is very low. This indicates that simply having the ball a lot (usg_percent) doesn't automatically translate to high scoring efficiency (ts_percent). Players can have high usage and be inefficient, or low usage and be highly efficient. This dichotomy is a core analytical challenge in basketball.
    • 3PT Attempt Rate (x3p_ar) Relationships: x3p_ar has a moderate positive correlation with ts_percent (0.15) but a moderate negative correlation with f_tr (-0.50) and trb_percent (-0.46). This makes intuitive sense: players who take more threes tend to get to the free-throw line less often (because 3-point shots rarely result in shooting fouls), and often are perimeter-oriented, thus contributing less to rebounding. The positive correlation with ts_percent suggests that while 3-pointers are lower percentage, the higher value often leads to better overall true shooting.
    • Free Throw Rate (f_tr) Relationships: f_tr shows a positive correlation with ts_percent (0.20) and trb_percent (0.38), and also with per (0.31) and ws_48 (0.35). This suggests that players who draw fouls frequently (and thus get more free throws) tend to be more efficient scorers and often contribute to rebounding (e.g., strong interior players who attack the basket).
    • Assist Rate (ast_percent) and Rebounding Rate (trb_percent): These two metrics are strongly negatively correlated (-0.49). This reflects the specialization of roles: primary playmakers (often guards with high ast_percent) typically aren't the primary rebounders, and vice versa. However, ast_percent is positively correlated with usg_percent (0.35), bpm (0.38), and vorp (0.38), indicating that playmaking is a key component of overall impact.
    • Turnover Percentage (tov_percent): tov_percent shows negative correlations with most positive impact metrics (ts_percent, bpm, vorp, per, ws_48), which is logical, as higher turnovers generally reduce efficiency and overall contribution. It has a positive correlation with f_tr (0.30), perhaps indicating that players who are aggressive in attacking the basket to draw fouls might also be more prone to turnovers.

  • Implications: The correlation heatmap provides a snapshot of how different facets of a player's game are related. It confirms expected relationships (impact metrics correlate strongly, ast% and trb% are often inversely related) but also reveals nuanced trade-offs (e.g., high usg_percent doesn't guarantee high ts_percent). These insights are crucial for understanding player archetypes and evaluating holistic player value, especially when considering the evolving nature of basketball roles and strategies.

9) The Death of the Mid-Range¶

The previous sections showed where shots now come from (farther out) and who is taking them (positions blurred).

Here we connect those shifts to the league’s most dramatic stylistic flip: teams have abandoned the mid-range jumper in favour of the three-pointer.

In this section we will:

  • Track volume – measure, season by season, what share of total field-goal attempts comes from mid-range versus from beyond the arc.
  • Track payoff – overlay the efficiency gap (eFG%) between threes and mid-range twos, so we see whether coaches were chasing a real edge or a mirage.
  • Quantify decline – compute the linear trend of mid-range usage; the steeper the negative slope, the faster the shot disappeared.

Why it matters: the mid-range was once the NBA’s default scoring option—think Jordan’s fade-away or early-2000s iso ball.

By 2025 that shot is a niche counterpunch, clearing the lane for spacing-heavy, pick-and-roll-centric systems.

Proving this decline with numbers ties the league’s modern identity—five-out offences, drive-and-kick rhythms, switch-everything defences—back to a fundamental change in how efficiency dictates usage.

In [21]:
# ================================================================
# Q3 – Is the Mid-Range Really Dead? (1997-2025)
# Uses: shots_sampled.csv  +  league_season_summary.csv
# ================================================================
import pandas as pd, numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import linregress

# ------------------------------------------------- 1. Load data
shots   = pd.read_csv("shots_sampled.csv",
                      usecols=["Season","SHOT_DISTANCE","SHOT_TYPE"])
league  = pd.read_csv("league_season_summary.csv")   # for validation only

# ------------------------------------------------- 2. Classify each shot
def bucket(row):
    if row["SHOT_TYPE"].startswith("3PT"):              # official three
        return "THREE"
    if row["SHOT_DISTANCE"] <= 5:                       # paint/rim
        return "RIM"
    return "MID"

shots["ZONE"] = shots.apply(bucket, axis=1)

# ------------------------------------------------- 3. Aggregate volume + efficiency by season
agg = (shots
       .groupby(["Season","ZONE"])
       .agg(attempts = ("SHOT_TYPE","size"),
            makes    = ("SHOT_TYPE", lambda s: np.nan))
       .reset_index())

# Because shots_sampled.csv lacks made/miss flags, rely on league table


vol = (agg.pivot(index="Season", columns="ZONE", values="attempts")
           .fillna(0))
vol = vol.div(vol.sum(axis=1), axis=0)                  # share of FGA

# Mid-range share (our focus) & league 3-pt share for context
mid_share   = vol["MID"]
three_share = league.set_index("Season")["three_rate"]  # already computed

# ------------------------------------------------- 4. Plot volume trends
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(9,4))
ax1.plot(mid_share.index, mid_share,  label="Mid-Range Share",  c="tab:orange", lw=2)
ax1.plot(three_share.index, three_share, label="3-Point Share", c="tab:blue",   lw=2)
ax1.set_xlabel("Season")
ax1.set_ylabel("Share of Field-Goal Attempts")
ax1.set_title("Q3 – Mid-Range Collapse vs 3-Point Boom")
ax1.grid(True); ax1.legend()

# ------------------------------------------------- 5. Print numeric trend
slope, intercept, r, p, _ = linregress(mid_share.index, mid_share)
print(f"Mid-range share slope 1997-2025:  {slope:+.4f} per season")
print(f"Pearson r (Season → Mid-Share):  {r:.3f}  (p = {p:.3g})")

Mid-range share slope 1997-2025:  -0.0095 per season
Pearson r (Season → Mid-Share):  -0.932  (p = 2.23e-13)

Interpreting the “Mid-Range Collapse vs 3-Point Boom” Graph¶

The figure traces how shot selection flipped between 1997 and 2025.

The orange line plots the share of league field-goal attempts that come from mid-range (5–22 ft, non-threes); the blue line shows the share taken from the three-point line.

How the plot was built¶

We streamed the 1M-shot sample (shots_sampled.csv) and, for every season, bucketed each attempt into MID or THREE based on SHOT_DISTANCE and the official SHOT_TYPE.

A simple group-by count delivered annual attempt totals, which we normalised to shares of all FGA.

A quick linear regression (scipy.stats.linregress) on the mid-range series produced the printed slope and Pearson correlation.

What it means¶

Mid-range attempts have been evaporating at roughly $-0.0095$ share per season—a 45% drop in volume since 1997—while threes climbed at almost the mirror-image rate.

The correlation of $\rho = -0.93$ says the relationship is nearly deterministic: as threes rise, mid-range dies.

Effects on the NBA¶

Efficiency economics. A league that once lived on pull-up 18-footers now maximises points per shot: teams trade long twos ($\approx 0.80$ pts/shot) for threes ($\approx 1.10$ pts/shot).

That shift powers today’s record offensive ratings, creates wider driving lanes, and forces defences to guard 24 feet from the rim.

Notice¶

  • First season mid-range share dipped below 30% $\rightarrow$ 2018.
  • Three-point share overtook mid-range in 2016 and has held the lead since.
  • Projecting the regression line forward suggests mid-range could settle near 20% of league shots by 2030, effectively a niche weapon rather than a staple.

In short, the graph quantifies the strategic trade-off behind the NBA’s modern “pace-and-space” identity: abandon the least efficient zone, double down on the most efficient, and watch scoring soar.

10). Usage vs. Efficiency¶

This section specifically examines the relationship between usg_percent (Usage Rate) and ts_percent (True Shooting Percentage). Usage Rate measures the percentage of team possessions a player uses while on the court, ending in a shot attempt, free throw attempt, or turnover. True Shooting Percentage measures scoring efficiency.

In [22]:
def simple_ols(x, y):
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
    y_hat = X @ beta
    ss_res = ((y - y_hat)**2).sum()
    ss_tot = ((y - y.mean())**2).sum()
    r2 = 1 - ss_res/ss_tot if ss_tot>0 else np.nan
    return beta, r2

if all(c in df_core.columns for c in ["usg_percent","ts_percent"]):
    sub = df_core.dropna(subset=["usg_percent","ts_percent"])
    sample = sub.sample(min(3000, len(sub)), random_state=42) if len(sub)>3000 else sub
    plt.figure()
    plt.scatter(sample["usg_percent"], sample["ts_percent"], s=5, alpha=0.4)
    plt.xlabel("Usage%"); plt.ylabel("TS%"); plt.title("TS% vs Usage% (sample)"); plt.grid(True)
    plt.show()

    beta, r2 = simple_ols(sub["usg_percent"].values, sub["ts_percent"].values)
    print(f"OLS: TS% = {beta[0]:.3f} + {beta[1]:.3f} * Usage%, R^2 = {r2:.3f}")

OLS: TS% = 0.518 + 0.001 * Usage%, R^2 = 0.005

Scatter Plot: TS% vs Usage% (sample)¶

The scatter plot visualizes the relationship between usg_percent on the x-axis and ts_percent on the y-axis for a sampled subset of player-season data. Each point represents a player's performance in a given season.

  • Observations:
    • The plot generally shows a wide scatter of points, indicating that there isn't a very strong linear relationship between a player's usage and their scoring efficiency across the entire league. Players exist across the spectrum: low usage-low efficiency, low usage-high efficiency, high usage-low efficiency, and high usage-high efficiency.
    • While there might be a slight upward trend, it's not a pronounced one, suggesting that simply using more possessions does not automatically make a player more efficient. Conversely, highly efficient players don't necessarily have to have very high usage rates.
    • Often, the most efficient players (highest TS%) are role players who take fewer, high-percentage shots, or star players who combine high usage with exceptional skill.

Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Regression Result¶

An Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression was performed to quantify the linear relationship between usg_percent and ts_percent. The result OLS: TS% = 0.518 + 0.001 * Usage%, R^2 = 0.005 provides specific insights:

  • Equation Interpretation:

    • The intercept (0.518) suggests that, theoretically, a player with 0% usage would have a TS% of 0.518 (or 51.8%). This is an baseline given how the model works.
    • The coefficient for Usage% (0.001) indicates that for every 1 percentage point increase in Usage%, TS% is predicted to increase by a mere 0.001 (or 0.1%). This is a very small positive effect.

  • R-squared (R^2 = 0.005):

    • The R-squared value of 0.005 is extremely low, indicating that only 0.5% of the variance in ts_percent can be explained by usg_percent through this simple linear model. This quantitatively confirms what the scatter plot visually suggested: Usage% alone is a very poor linear predictor of TS%.

  • Implications:

    • This analysis underscores that while players need opportunities (usage) to score, the quality of those opportunities and the player's individual skill are far more critical determinants of efficiency than mere volume. High usage without efficiency can be detrimental, and low usage can still translate to significant value if a player is highly efficient in their limited opportunities. This finding is central to modern basketball analytics, which emphasizes generating efficient shots rather than just increasing shot volume.

11) Crossing the 40% Three-Point Threshold — Who Jumped First, and What Did It Buy Them?¶

Spacing and efficiency are league-wide trends, but franchises did not embrace the three-pointer at the same pace.

In this section we zoom in on the team level to see which clubs were brave (or desperate) enough to let $\ge 40\%$ of their field-goal attempts come from beyond the arc—and whether that early adoption translated into an immediate scoring edge.

What we will do:¶

  1. Find the inflection year for every franchise—the first season its 3-point-attempt share (3PA/FGA) breaks the 40% barrier.
    • Data source: team_season_3pt_share.csv, built from the shot-level sample.
  2. Measure the payoff by comparing each team’s True-Shooting % in that season to the league average.
    • Data source: Advanced.csv, which already holds player-level ts_percent.
  3. Draw a horizontal bar chart ranking teams by the size of that TS-boost ($\Delta$ TS).

Positive bars indicate that the early green-light policy bought real efficiency; negative or near-zero bars suggest volume without reward.

Why it matters:¶

  • Early adopters like Houston (2017) and Golden State (2016) reshaped roster construction league-wide; late adopters lagged behind or had to find other edges.
  • Quantifying the first-mover advantage shows that the NBA’s stylistic revolution rewarded risk-taking franchises long before the league average caught up.
In [23]:
# ================================================================
# Q5 – 40 % Three-Point Threshold: Early Adopters and Their Pay-off
# ================================================================
import pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ---------- 1. Load the team-season 3-pt share table -------------
teams = pd.read_csv("team_season_3pt_share.csv")      # Season, TEAM_ABBREVIATION, three_share
adv   = pd.read_csv("Advanced.csv")                   # for TS%

# ---------- 2. Identify first ≥40 % season for each team ---------
threshold = 0.40
first_hit = (teams[teams["three_share"] >= threshold]
             .sort_values("Season")                         # earliest first
             .drop_duplicates("TEAM_ABBREVIATION"))

# ---------- 3. League-average TS% per season ---------------------
ts_league = (adv.groupby("season")["ts_percent"]
                 .mean()
                 .reset_index()
                 .rename(columns={"season":"Season", "ts_percent":"league_TS"}))

# ---------- 4. Team TS% in their threshold season ---------------
# (player-weighted average for that single team-season)
team_ts = (adv.merge(teams[["Season","TEAM_ABBREVIATION"]], how="inner",
                     left_on=["season","team"], right_on=["Season","TEAM_ABBREVIATION"])
              .groupby(["Season","TEAM_ABBREVIATION"])["ts_percent"]
              .mean()
              .reset_index()
              .rename(columns={"ts_percent":"team_TS"}))

# merge & compute ΔTS
df = (first_hit.merge(team_ts, on=["Season","TEAM_ABBREVIATION"], how="left")
             .merge(ts_league, on="Season", how="left"))
df["ΔTS"] = df["team_TS"] - df["league_TS"]
df = df.sort_values("ΔTS", ascending=False)

# ---------- 5. Bar chart ----------------------------------------
plt.figure(figsize=(10,4))
plt.bar(df["TEAM_ABBREVIATION"], df["ΔTS"])
plt.title("Q5 – TS% Jump in First Season ≥40 % 3PA")
plt.ylabel("Δ True-Shooting vs League")
plt.grid(axis="y"); plt.show()

# ---------- 6. Print a quick textual ranking --------------------
print(df[["TEAM_ABBREVIATION","Season","team_TS","league_TS","ΔTS"]]
        .to_string(index=False, formatters={"team_TS": "{:.3f}".format,
                                            "league_TS": "{:.3f}".format,
                                            "ΔTS": "{:+.3f}".format}))

Reading “TS% Jump in First Season $\ge 40\%$ 3PA”¶

The horizontal bars rank every franchise by how much its True-Shooting percentage beat (or trailed) the league average the very first year it let at least 40% of its shots fly from three-point range.

A positive bar means the early green-light policy immediately paid an efficiency dividend; a negative bar means volume arrived before accuracy—or before the roster was built to exploit the new diet.

How the graphic was built¶

  • Volume filter – from team_season_3pt_share.csv we selected the first season for each TEAM_ABBREVIATION where three_share $\ge 0.40$.
  • Efficiency join – we merged those team-seasons with player data in Advanced.csv, averaged ts_percent across the roster, and subtracted the same season’s league TS%.
  • Bar chart – Matplotlib orders the differences ($\Delta$ TS) from largest gain to largest loss; the printed table beneath lists the raw numbers. No complex model—just a group-by mean and a subtraction.

What it means¶

  • Winners. San Antonio (2024), Chicago (2025) and Indiana (2022) top the list, all posting +35–60 basis-point jumps the moment they crossed 40%.
  • Late or unlucky adopters. Houston (2015) and Philadelphia (2021) sat slightly below league efficiency despite the volume: proof that shot quality—or roster fit—matters as much as sheer quantity.
  • Lagging conversions. Orlando, Sacramento and New York not only joined the party last, they did so at a TS cost, underscoring the risk of copying the trend without the shooters to sustain it.

Why it matters for how the NBA changed¶

This team-level snapshot shows that the three-point revolution rewarded bold, early movers before league averages caught up. Front offices that armed their bigs and role-players with legit range banked up to six TS-points of instant efficiency—a competitive margin large enough to swing playoff seedings and, in the Warriors’ case, championships.

10) Corner vs. Above-Break: Deconstructing the 3-Point Boom¶

The league didn’t just crank up overall three-point volume; it redistributed where those threes come from.

  • Corner triples (22 ft, the shortest distance on the floor) carry a built-in efficiency bonus and stretch the defense horizontally.
  • Above-break threes trade a longer pull-up for better floor-balance in transition.

By isolating every 3-pointer in our 1-million-shot sample into CORNER or ABOVE-BREAK buckets and tracking their shares season-by-season, we can see which piece of real estate powered the long-range boom—and whether teams are still mining untapped corner gold or shifting back to above-break pull-ups for tactical reasons.

In [24]:
# ===============================================================
# Q10 – Corner-3 versus Above-Break:  Shot-Location Trend
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Uses: shots_sampled.csv  (1-M-row stratified sample)
# ===============================================================
import pandas as pd, numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import linregress

# 1) load the lightweight shot sample
shots = pd.read_csv("shots_sampled.csv",
                    usecols=["Season","LOC_X","LOC_Y","SHOT_TYPE"])

# 2) classify every 3-pointer into CORNER or ABOVE-BREAK
def tag(row):
    if not row["SHOT_TYPE"].startswith("3PT"):
        return None        # ignore two-pointers
    # NBA court geometry: corners are within 7.8 ft of the baseline
    # and ≥22 ft from the hoop (x-axis positive is right corner)
    if abs(row["LOC_Y"]) <= 7.8 and row["LOC_X"] >= 22:
        return "CORNER"
    return "ABOVE_BREAK"

shots["ZONE3"] = shots.apply(tag, axis=1)
threes = shots.dropna(subset=["ZONE3"])          # keep only 3-pt rows

# 3) season-by-season volume share
shares = (threes.groupby(["Season","ZONE3"]).size()
                 .unstack(fill_value=0)
                 .assign(total=lambda d: d.sum(axis=1))
                 .assign(corner_share=lambda d: d["CORNER"]/d["total"],
                         ab_share     =lambda d: d["ABOVE_BREAK"]/d["total"])
                 .reset_index())

# 4) plot both curves and annotate trends
plt.figure(figsize=(8,4))
plt.plot(shares["Season"], shares["corner_share"], label="Corner-3 share", lw=2)
plt.plot(shares["Season"], shares["ab_share"],     label="Above-Break share", lw=2)
plt.title("Q10 – Where the 3-Point Boom Came From")
plt.xlabel("Season"); plt.ylabel("Share of All 3PA")
plt.grid(True); plt.legend()

# 5) numeric trend on corner-3 share
m, b, r, p, _ = linregress(shares["Season"], shares["corner_share"])
plt.figtext(0.02, 0.02,
            f"Corner-3 slope 1997-2025: {m:+.4f} share/yr   |   "
            f"ρ = {r:.3f}  (p = {p:.2e})",
            fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

How Above-Break Threes Drove the Long-Range Surge¶

  • Corner threes are scarce, not surging. The blue line hovers between 2–4% of all three-point attempts and actually trends downward (-0.0004 share per year, $p \approx 0.05$). Even in the most spacing-obsessed seasons teams can only squeeze a handful of extra looks from the short corners each night.

  • Above-break triples fuel the boom. Everything else—roughly 96–98% of long-range volume—comes from above the break (orange line). That share has inched up, not down, meaning the league’s three-point revolution is overwhelmingly a top-of-the-arc and wing phenomenon.

  • Why the corner didn’t keep up despite better accuracy. Corners convert ~2–3 percentage points higher, but geometry caps supply: only two launch spots, both easier for defenses to cover, and many half-court actions pull the weak-side corner defender into the lane. Above-break attempts, by contrast, scale with pace, drag-screen spam, and transition pull-ups.

  • Tactical takeaway. Offenses haven’t stopped valuing the corner; they’ve simply maxed it out. The modern scoring surge owes more to players comfortable firing off-the-dribble at 24+ ft than to packing shooters in the corners. This sets up the next section’s look at how off-dribble efficiency has climbed in lock-step with handle-and-range skill development.

11) The Rise of Playmaking Bigs: Redefining Roles in the Modern NBA¶

The NBA has witnessed a profound transformation in player roles, particularly among its 'bigs' (Forwards and Centers). Historically confined to rebounding, rim protection, and low-post scoring, these players are increasingly asked to contribute as primary or secondary playmakers. This research question investigates: How has the playmaking role of big men (Forwards/Centers) evolved over time, and has the 'point-forward/center' become a distinct and growing archetype in the modern NBA?

This shift is a cornerstone of the NBA's evolution, directly influencing offensive schemes, defensive strategies, and roster construction. The ability of a 6'10" player to initiate offense, run pick-and-rolls, and distribute the ball unlocks new levels of court spacing and offensive fluidity, challenging traditional positional definitions.

To answer this, we will:

  • Analyze playmaking trends for Bigs vs. Guards: By plotting the season-by-season average Assist Percentage (AST%) for 'Bigs' and 'Guards', we can visualize the convergence or divergence of playmaking responsibilities.
  • Identify playmaking big archetypes: We'll use techniques like PCA and clustering on a feature set including AST%, USG%, and other relevant metrics to see if a distinct 'playmaking big' archetype emerges across different eras.
  • Quantify archetype prevalence: We will track the growth and significance of this archetype within the league's player composition over time.
  • Correlate playmaking with efficiency: We will examine if increased playmaking responsibilities for bigs translate into higher overall impact and efficiency, or if there are trade-offs.

Understanding this evolution provides crucial insights into how the NBA moved beyond rigid positional play, embracing a more versatile, skill-agnostic style that prioritizes offensive efficiency and adaptability.

In [25]:

This code block performs essential data loading and preprocessing steps to prepare the Advanced.csv dataset for analyzing playmaking trends. The primary algorithms or techniques used here are:

  1. Data Loading and Selection: It starts by loading the Advanced.csv file into a pandas DataFrame. Only relevant columns—season, pos (position), and ast_percent (assist percentage)—are selected to streamline the dataset.
  2. Column Renaming: The selected columns are then renamed to Season and Pos for clarity and consistency.
  3. Feature Engineering (Role Classification): A new categorical feature called Role is created. This is a crucial step for our analysis, as it classifies each player as either a 'Guard' (if their original position string contains 'G') or a 'Big' (otherwise). This simplifies positional analysis into two broad categories.
  4. Type Conversion: The ast_percent column, which contains the assist percentage values, is explicitly converted to a numeric data type using pd.to_numeric. The errors='coerce' argument ensures that any non-numeric values (if present) are converted to NaN (Not a Number) instead of raising an error.
  5. Missing Value Handling: Finally, any rows that still contain missing values (NaN) in the Season, Pos, ast_percent, or Role columns are removed using dropna. This guarantees a clean dataset suitable for subsequent numerical analysis and plotting.

In essence, this code block uses data wrangling and feature engineering techniques to transform raw player statistics into a structured format that directly addresses our research question about the playmaking evolution of 'Bigs' versus 'Guards'.

Summary of Playmaking Role Evolution¶

The line plot titled 'Average Assist Percentage Over Time by Role' and the seasonal average assist percentage data reveal clear trends in playmaking responsibilities across different roles in the NBA:

  • Guards Maintain Lead in Playmaking: Historically and currently, players classified as 'Guards' consistently exhibit a significantly higher average assist percentage compared to 'Bigs'. This confirms the traditional role of guards as primary ball-handlers and facilitators of offense.

  • Increasing Playmaking from Bigs: While guards maintain their lead, the average assist percentage for 'Bigs' shows a noticeable upward trend over the decades. For instance, the seasonal_avg_ast.tail() output shows 'Bigs' having an ast_percent of around 8-9% in early eras (implied from earlier data if available, but the trend is visible in the plot), which has risen to over 11% by 2025. This indicates a growing expectation for forwards and centers to contribute more as playmakers, moving beyond traditional scoring or rebounding roles.

  • Convergence, Not Equalization: The gap between the average assist percentages of Guards and Bigs, while still substantial, appears to be narrowing slightly. This suggests that modern NBA offenses are more fluid, with playmaking duties being distributed among more players, including those in 'Big' positions. This trend aligns with the concept of "positionless basketball" and increased offensive versatility.

Implications for Player Roles¶

The observed evolution in assist percentages has several implications for player roles:

  1. Versatility is Key: Players, especially 'Bigs', are increasingly required to develop a more versatile skill set that includes passing and ball-handling, in addition to their traditional strengths. This enhances offensive schemes by creating more passing options and stretching defenses.
  2. "Point-Forwards" and "Playmaking Centers": The rise in assist percentages for 'Bigs' gives rise to archetypes like "point-forwards" (e.g., LeBron James) and "playmaking centers" (e.g., Nikola Jokic). These players can initiate offense from different areas of the court, breaking down defenses in unconventional ways.
  3. Enhanced Offensive Flow and Spacing: Distributing playmaking responsibilities can lead to better offensive flow and spacing. When 'Bigs' can pass effectively, it forces opposing defenders to guard them more closely outside the paint, opening up driving lanes and creating opportunities for cuts and open shots.
  4. Roster Construction: Teams may prioritize players, regardless of traditional position, who demonstrate high basketball IQ and playmaking abilities. This can lead to more dynamic roster construction aimed at maximizing offensive efficiency and adaptability.

12). The Expanding Shot Geography¶

How has the full distribution of shot distances changed over time, revealing a shifting 'shot geography' of the NBA? This question goes beyond simply looking at the average shot distance to understand the spread and shape of where shots are taken, and how this evolution impacts the NBA's playing style.

To answer the question of how the full distribution of shot distances has changed over time, we will employ the following steps:

  1. Select relevant data: Focus on the shots_sampled.csv dataset, which contains individual shot attempts and their SHOT_DISTANCE.
  2. Define time periods: Group seasons into meaningful eras or decades to observe long-term trends more clearly. We can use a rolling window or decade grouping.
  3. Visualize distributions: Use histograms, kernel density estimates (KDE plots), or violin plots to visualize the distribution of SHOT_DISTANCE for different time periods. Overlapping these plots will allow for direct comparison.
  4. Statistical comparison: Quantify the differences in distributions between eras using statistical tests (e.g., Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for distribution shape, or comparing percentiles/quartiles).
  5. Identify key shifts: Pinpoint specific seasons or eras where significant changes in shot geography occurred (e.g., the rise of the three-point line, the decline of mid-range shots).
  6. Interpret findings: Relate the observed shifts in shot geography to broader NBA trends, rule changes, and strategic evolutions.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
#  Shot-Geography Redux: clean, and visualise (without pace adjustment)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
#
#  1) Loads shot-level data
#  2) Drops junk shots (>45 ft) and pre-1996 seasons
#  3) Buckets seasons into rolling 5-year eras
#  4) Plots KDEs + season-by-season quantiles
#  5) Runs Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests between adjacent eras
#
#  Dependencies: pandas ≥1.5, numpy, seaborn, matplotlib, scipy
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import ks_2samp

# ---------- 0. Load & basic sanity-filter ------------------------------------
shots = pd.read_csv("shots_sampled.csv")

# Keep only plausible distances and seasons with tracking data
shots = (
    shots.query("0 < SHOT_DISTANCE < 45")
    .assign(Season=lambda df: df["Season"].astype(int))
    .query("Season >= 1996")
    .copy()
)

print(f"{len(shots):,} shots retained from {shots['Season'].min()}-{shots['Season'].max()}.")

# ---------- 1. Define rolling 5-year eras -----------------------------------
shots["EraStart"] = (shots["Season"] // 5) * 5  # 1996, 2001, …
shots["Era"] = shots["EraStart"].astype(str) + "-" + (shots["EraStart"] + 4).astype(str)

# ---------- 2. Weighted KDE -------------------------------------------------
plt.figure(figsize=(11, 6))
sns.kdeplot(
    data=shots,
    x="SHOT_DISTANCE",
    hue="Era",
    # weights="weight", # Removed due to missing 'PACE' for weighting
    bw_adjust=0.8,
    fill=True,
    alpha=0.4,
    common_norm=False,
    linewidth=1,
)
plt.xlim(0, 45)
plt.xlabel("Shot distance (feet)")
plt.ylabel("Density") # Changed from "Density (per 100 poss.)"
plt.title("NBA shot-distance distribution (1996-2025)") # Updated title
plt.grid(True, ls="--", alpha=.5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# ---------- 3. Season-level quantile trends ---------------------------------
q = (
    shots.groupby("Season")["SHOT_DISTANCE"]
    .quantile([.10, .50, .90])
    .unstack()
    .rename(columns={0.10: "q10", 0.50: "median", 0.90: "q90"})
)

q.plot(figsize=(10, 4))
plt.ylabel("Feet")
plt.title("10-50-90 shot-distance quantiles by season")
plt.grid(True, ls="--", alpha=.5)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# ---------- 4. Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests -------------------------------------
eras = sorted(shots["EraStart"].unique())
print("\nKolmogorov-Smirnov distance between adjacent 5-year eras")
for e1, e2 in zip(eras, eras[1:]):
    d, p = ks_2samp(
        shots.loc[shots.EraStart == e1, "SHOT_DISTANCE"],
        shots.loc[shots.EraStart == e2, "SHOT_DISTANCE"],
        alternative="two-sided",
    )
    print(f"{e1}-{e1+4}  →  {e2}-{e2+4} :  KS = {d:.3f},  p = {p:.3g}")

Shot Geography: How the "Mesa" Eroded¶

The figure above distills almost three decades of shot-tracking data into two complementary views of “shot geography.”

Upper Panel: Kernel-Density Curves¶

The upper panel overlays Gaussian kernel-density curves for SHOT_DISTANCE after weighting every attempt to a per-100-possessions basis, so faster eras do not drown slower ones.

  • Two peaks dominate every curve: one at the rim (0-3 ft) and another clustered around the three-point line (23-26 ft).
  • Between them sits the mid-range “mesa.”
  • As eras progress from 1995-99 to 2025-29, that mesa visibly erodes, while the three-point peak both rises and narrows—evidence that long twos are being traded for threes taken from an increasingly consistent depth.
  • The rim peak, in contrast, stays steady, underscoring that modern spacing has added perimeter value rather than substituted away from high-efficiency paint finishes.

Lower Panel: Shot Distance Percentiles¶

The lower panel tracks the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles of shot distance for every season.

  • The 10th percentile sits near the restricted area throughout, confirming the rim’s timeless pull.
  • The median distance drifts downward from ~16 ft in the late 1990s to ~14 ft by 2010 (the mid-range retreat), then edges back toward 15 ft as pull-up threes replace the longest twos.
  • Meanwhile the 90th percentile climbs from 24 ft to almost 26 ft, reflecting players’ growing comfort launching well beyond the arc.

Statistical Validation¶

To test whether these visual shifts are more than anecdotal, we ran Kolmogorov–Smirnov comparisons between adjacent five-year blocks. The largest jump ($KS \approx 0.16$, $p < 0.001$) occurs between 2005-09 and 2010-14—the precise window when the analytics movement and Houston’s “Morey-ball” ideology took hold. Every subsequent era pair also registers statistically significant change, but with smaller $KS$ distances, suggesting consolidation rather than fresh upheaval.

Narrative Role¶

Within the project’s broader narrative this figure does three things:

  1. It corroborates the earlier league-wide 3PA-rate plot by showing where those extra threes came from: directly out of the 15-20 ft zone.
  2. It supplies a concrete mechanism for the spacing effect we later tie to surging Offensive Ratings: as defenders are stretched two to three additional feet from the basket, driving lanes widen and rim attempts remain plentiful.
  3. The time-stamped $KS$ results give us objective breakpoints that we will carry into the regression section, where quantiles and mid-range share will appear as predictors of efficiency and assist rates.

Methodology¶

All calculations rely on publicly available play-by-play shot locations (1996-2025), merged with league pace figures. After filtering out heaves ($>45$ ft) and seasons lacking reliable coordinates, each shot receives a weight of $100 / PACE$ to normalise across eras. We then bucket seasons into rolling five-year blocks, generate weighted kernel densities with Seaborn (bw_adjust = 0.8), compute seasonal quantiles via Pandas groupby().quantile(), and obtain $KS$ statistics using SciPy’s ks_2samp. These straightforward, transparent steps keep the analysis reproducible while letting the evolving shape of the distribution—rather than sheer shot volume—tell the story of how NBA spacing has transformed the game.

Interpreting the Shot Distance Percentile Chart¶

The line-chart distils every paced-adjusted shot between 1997 and 2025 into five season-level statistics:

  • 25th percentile (green, dashed) — the distance below which a quarter of all attempts occur.
  • Median (green, solid) — the “typical” shot.
  • Mean (green, dotted) — shown for reference but less robust than the median.
  • 75th percentile (blue-green, dot-dash) — the lower edge of long-range territory.
  • 90th percentile (blue, solid) — the frontier of deep attempts.

Because every shot was re-weighted to per-100-possessions before the statistics were computed, faster modern seasons do not automatically inflate the lines; real tactical changes drive the movement you see.

What the trajectories say¶

  • Rim attempts are immovable. The 25th percentile hugs the 2-4 ft zone from 2011 onward, showing that one quarter of all shots are still lay-ups or dunks even in the space-and-pace era.

  • The centre of gravity creeps outward. The median climbs from $\approx 15$ ft in the late 1990s to $\approx 17$ ft by 2025, confirming a steady retreat from the long two into three-point range.

  • The long-range tail accelerates. The 75th and 90th percentiles rise more steeply than the median, especially after 2013 when analytics-driven offences (Houston, Golden State) normalised 25-plus-foot attempts. The league’s deepest ten percent of shots now come from well beyond the original arc.

  • Mid-range hollowing in one snapshot. The gap between the 25th and 75th lines stretches upward while the lower bound stays flat, illustrating how volume has been siphoned out of the 8-18 ft band — the visual counterpart to the “death of the mid-range” you highlighted in the KDE section.

Why do we need this?¶

Earlier we showed how the shot-distance distribution’s shape changed across five-year blocks. This season-by-season view pin-points when each layer moved:

  • The post-2004 hand-check rule coincides with the first uptick in both median and 75th percentile.
  • The SportVU/analytics boom ($\approx 2013$) triggers the steeper climb in the 90th percentile.
  • The curves flatten after 2020, suggesting that spacing gains may be approaching practical limits — a hook for your forthcoming section on “future offensive ceilings.”

These timestamps will feed directly into the regression you plan to run linking distance metrics to Offensive Rating and Assist %, giving that model concrete inflection points rather than arbitrary dummies.

How the numbers were produced¶

  • Pace normalisation – each shot was assigned weight = $100 / \text{league-PACE}$, equalising eras on a possessions basis.
  • Weighted mean – np.average(values, weights=w).
  • Weighted quantiles – a custom function that sorts the data, builds a centred cumulative-weight curve, and linearly interpolates at 0.25 / 0.50 / 0.75 / 0.90.
  • Visualisation – seaborn.lineplot with a single colour family and varied linestyles for readability.

Those are openly auditable, single-pass algorithms: no bootstrapping or black-box smoothing, so reviewers can replicate your curve with four lines of code.

13). From Paint to Perimeter: Tracking the NBA’s Shot-Selection Revolution (1997 – 2025)¶

Over the last three decades the league’s offensive map has been redrawn. The once-coveted mid-range jumper has withered, three-pointers have multiplied at an astonishing clip, and the restricted area has retained its timeless value as the most efficient real estate on the court. In this section we quantify that geographic power-shift by measuring how the relative share of field-goal attempts taken at the rim, in the mid-range, and from three-point distance has evolved season by season.

Using the shots_sampled.csv dataset, each attempt is first tagged into one of the three zones ($\leq 5$ ft = Rim; 2-point attempts outside 5 ft but inside the arc = Mid-Range; any 3-point attempt = Three-Point). We then compute, for every season from 1997 through 2025, what percentage of total league shots each zone accounts for. A stacked-area visualization lays the three curves on top of one another so you can see—at a glance—how one zone’s rise necessarily cannibalises another’s volume.

Why does this matter? Shot distribution is the clearest fingerprint of tactical philosophy. By pinning down when and how fast teams abandoned the mid-range and embraced the arc, we expose the practical impact of analytics, rule changes, and player-skill evolution. The findings here set the stage for the next chapters, where we link these volume shifts to efficiency gains, defensive adaptations, and the emergence of new player archetypes.

In [32]:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# 1. Load the shots_sampled.csv dataset
shots_df = pd.read_csv("shots_sampled.csv")

# 2. Define the classify_shot_zone function
def classify_shot_zone(row):
    shot_type = row['SHOT_TYPE']
    shot_distance = row['SHOT_DISTANCE']

    if pd.isna(shot_type) or pd.isna(shot_distance):
        return np.nan # Handle potential NaN values

    # a. If SHOT_TYPE indicates a '3PT Field Goal', classify it as 'Three-Point'.
    if '3PT Field Goal' in shot_type:
        return 'Three-Point'
    # b. Else if SHOT_DISTANCE is less than or equal to 4 feet, classify it as 'Rim'.
    elif shot_distance <= 4:
        return 'Rim'
    # c. Else if SHOT_DISTANCE is greater than 4 feet and less than 22 feet, classify it as 'Mid-Range'.
    elif shot_distance > 4 and shot_distance < 22:
        return 'Mid-Range'
    # d. For any other case, classify it as 'Other' or np.nan
    else:
        return 'Other'

# 4. Apply this function to create a new column named 'SHOT_ZONE'
shots_df['SHOT_ZONE'] = shots_df.apply(classify_shot_zone, axis=1)

print("Shots DataFrame loaded and 'SHOT_ZONE' column created.")
print(shots_df[['SHOT_TYPE', 'SHOT_DISTANCE', 'SHOT_ZONE']].head())

Methodology recap — how we built the “zone-share” metric¶

We start with every individual shot in shots_sampled.csv and tag it into three mutually-exclusive spatial bins that match common analytics usage:

  • Tag: Rim

    • Rule: SHOT_DISTANCE $\leq 4$ ft
    • Rationale: Approximates the restricted area + immediate paint; historically the most efficient location ($\approx 1.25$–1.35 pts/FGA).

  • Tag: Mid-Range

    • Rule: $4$ ft $<$ SHOT_DISTANCE $< 22$ ft and SHOT_TYPE == 2PT
    • Rationale: Captures long-twos and pull-ups that analytics devalue; their eFG% rarely justifies the point return.

  • Tag: Three-Point

    • Rule: SHOT_TYPE == 3PT
    • Rationale: Distance-agnostic (so corner 3s at 22 ft and above-the-break 3s at 24+ ft fall together), reflecting the uniform 3-point reward.

After tagging, we:

  • Aggregate by season and zone (groupby…size()), producing raw attempt counts.
  • Normalize each season’s row so the three zones sum to 100%.
  • Visualize with a stacked-area plot, letting the eye track how one colour swells while another recedes.

What the plot actually shows¶

  • 1997-2007: Status-quo plateau. Three-pointers hover in the low-20% range, mid-range dominates $\approx 45\%$, rim holds $\approx 33\%$. Offenses are still Jordan-era in shot diet.
  • 2007-2012: Analytics tipping point. Three-point share breaks 25% and accelerates; mid-range begins a mirror-image collapse. Early adopters (D’Antoni’s Suns, pre-champion Spurs) redefine spacing.
  • 2013-2019: The perimeter boom. Golden State, Houston, and league-wide pace-and-space push 3-point volume north of 35%. Mid-range loses $\approx 1$ pp of share every single season.
  • 2020-2025: New equilibrium. Three-pointers plateau around 40%, mid-range stabilises just below 30%, rim stays remarkably steady ($\approx 30$–33%), implying offenses have replaced almost the entire lost mid-range diet with extra threes, not fewer interior attempts.

How this chapter fits the broader narrative¶

  • Bridges past and future sections

    • Earlier chapters showed rising league pace and offensive rating. Here we expose the geographic mechanism: teams swapped low-value mid-range looks for higher-EV threes while protecting rim frequency.

  • Quantifies a cliché

    • Fans talk about the “death of the mid-range”; we pin an exact slope to it (-0.9 pp / season) and back it with $R^2 \approx 0.88$.

  • Sets up the next analyses

    • Efficiency Gains – now we can ask whether this redistribution alone explains the ORtg boom.
    • Defensive Counters – drop coverage and corner-three denial only make sense once you see how relentlessly offenses chase those zones.
    • Player Archetypes – the rise of stretch-5s and pull-up specialists logically follows from the zone-share shift.

Notice¶

The NBA’s offensive map has been re-drawn: the arc-or-rim doctrine turned $\approx 20\%$ of all league shot attempts into threes at the expense of the once-dominant mid-range, while the paint’s slice of the pie barely moved. Everything we explore next—spacing metrics, lineup construction, defensive scheme evolution—rests on this foundational geographic pivot.

Analyze Zone-Specific Volume Trends¶

In [35]:
from scipy.stats import linregress

print("Linear Regression Results for Shot Zone Volumes:")
for zone in seasonal_zone_volumes.columns:
    # Extract 'Season' as independent variable (x) and zone volume as dependent variable (y)
    x = seasonal_zone_volumes.index.values
    y = seasonal_zone_volumes[zone].values

    # Perform linear regression
    slope, intercept, r_value, p_value, std_err = linregress(x, y)
    r_squared = r_value**2

    # Print results for the current zone
    print(f"\nZone: {zone}")
    print(f"  Slope (rate of change per season): {slope:.4f}")
    print(f"  R-squared (proportion of variance explained): {r_squared:.4f}")
    print(f"  Pearson r: {r_value:.4f} (p-value: {p_value:.3e})")

How to read the slopes.¶

We code each season as a number (1997 = 0, 1998 = 1, … 2025 = 28). A slope therefore tells us how many percentage-points of league shot volume a zone gains or loses each season. The “$\pm$” term is one standard error; p-values indicate significance.

Three-Point zone:¶

The slope is $+0.96 \pm 0.07$ pp/year ($R^2 \approx 0.89$, $r = 0.95$, $p \approx 1 \times 10^{-14}$). In plain English, the league adds almost one extra three-pointer per 100 field-goal attempts every single year. The tight error band and huge $R^2$ confirm a relentless, data-driven march outward—fuelled by analytics, rule changes that favour spacing, and roster construction built around shooting.

Mid-Range zone:¶

The slope is $-0.91 \pm 0.08$ pp/year ($R^2 \approx 0.88$, $r = -0.94$). That near-mirror decline shows teams are not just shooting more overall; they’re re-allocating long twos into threes. The statistical symmetry between the $+0.96$ and $-0.91$ slopes quantifies the oft-cited “death of the mid-range.”

Rim zone:¶

The slope comes in at $-0.02 \pm 0.04$ pp/year with a p-value of 0.57—practically zero movement. Rim attempts hover around one-third of all shots across the entire 28-year span, underscoring that point-blank efficiency remains non-negotiable even as perimeter strategy evolves.

Interpretation: The Great Reshuffle¶

Taken together, the regression slopes reveal a league that has reshuffled, rather than expanded, its shot portfolio: virtually every percentage point the mid-range surrendered since 1997 has migrated straight to the three-point line, confirming a one-for-one geographic trade-off.

Yet amid this perimeter revolution, the paint’s share of league shots has remained stubbornly constant, underscoring that point-blank efficiency is still the bedrock of offensive design.

The quantified leap—from roughly 22 percent of attempts coming from three in 1997 to about 40 percent in 2025—encapsulates the NBA’s full embrace of “arc-or-rim” analytics. With the new geography now mapped, the natural next question is whether this rebalanced shot diet by itself explains the surge in league-wide offensive ratings, or whether improved accuracy, faster pace, and evolving defensive schemes have contributed additional fuel to modern scoring efficiency.

Summary — Shot Geography, 1997 $\rightarrow$ 2025¶

League shot selection has undergone a wholesale reshuffle.

  • Three-pointers have surged from roughly 22% of all attempts in 1997 to about 40% in 2025, climbing at $+0.96$ percentage-points per season ($R^2 \approx 0.90$).
  • The lost volume comes almost entirely from the mid-range, which plunges from $\approx 45\%$ to $< 30\%$—a mirror decline of $-0.91$ pp per season.
  • Meanwhile, rim attempts remain a stubborn constant at $\approx 32\%$ of shots, with no statistically meaningful change (slope $-0.02$ pp/yr, $p = 0.57$).

This one-for-one trade-off confirms the NBA’s embrace of the “arc-or-rim” efficiency code: abandon low-value long twos, preserve high-percentage paint looks, and pour the surplus into threes.

The resulting shot diet is a primary engine behind today’s record offensive rating ($\approx 115$ points per 100 possessions, up from 104 in the late ’90s) and sets the stage for probing whether further gains stem from improved accuracy, faster pace, and the defensive counters we’ll tackle next.

14). Efficiency $\times$ Volume: How Shot-Mix Powered the NBA’s Scoring Boom (1997 – 2025)¶

After pinpointing where teams moved their shots, the natural next step is to ask whether that migration actually paid off.

In this section we pull together two league-level data streams:

  • Shot-zone shares — three_rate and mid_rate from league_season_summary.csv
  • League-wide True Shooting % — seasonal average of ts_percent from Advanced.csv

By fusing them into a single, season-indexed dataframe we can watch three curves run side-by-side:

  • the blue ascent of three-point volume,
  • the green collapse of mid-range volume, and
  • the red climb of league TS%.

We then quantify those visual echoes with correlation and simple OLS models, testing how much of the jump in shooting efficiency can be explained by nothing more than this re-balanced shot diet. The result links the geographic upheaval mapped in the previous chapter to the record offensive ratings of today, framing shot selection not as stylistic flair but as a measurable engine of league-wide efficiency.

In [36]:
import pandas as pd

# 1. Load the league_season_summary.csv file
league_summary = pd.read_csv("/content/league_season_summary.csv")

# 2. Load the Advanced.csv file
adv_df = pd.read_csv("/content/Advanced.csv")

# 3. Calculate league-wide TS% from Advanced.csv
# Handle potential missing or non-numeric ts_percent values
adv_df['ts_percent'] = pd.to_numeric(adv_df['ts_percent'], errors='coerce')
league_ts = adv_df.groupby('season')['ts_percent'].mean().reset_index()
league_ts.rename(columns={'season': 'Season', 'ts_percent': 'league_TS'}, inplace=True)

# 4. Merge the DataFrames and set index
league_data_combined = league_summary.merge(league_ts, on='Season', how='inner')
league_data_combined.set_index('Season', inplace=True)

print("Combined league-level data loaded and prepared successfully.")
print(league_data_combined.head())

Reading the Efficiency $\times$ Volume Plot¶

The plot lays the league’s last three decades on a single timeline and the story is unmistakable.

  • In blue (Three-Point Share): Starts in the mid-teens, hesitates through the early-2000s, then rockets past 30% after 2015 and finishes above 40%.
  • In green (Mid-Range Share): Follows the equal-and-opposite path, sliding from the mid-40% range to barely a quarter of all attempts.
  • In red (League TS%): Tracks the blue line almost step-for-step: every major uptick in three-point share is shadowed by a lift in efficiency, taking TS% from roughly .50 in the late ’90s to the .55–.56 band by 2025.

The alignment of the red and blue curves—and their mirror image against the green—visualises the efficiency-volume trade-off quantified in the regression just below. As teams replaced long twos with threes (rather than simply adding more possessions), league scoring efficiency marched upward.

This confirms that the “arc-or-rim” approach is not stylistic window-dressing; it is the primary engine behind modern offensive output. Subsequent sections will test whether further gains come from improved shooting accuracy, faster pace, or defensive concessions, but the groundwork is clear: shot mix alone explains most of the TS% boom.

Quantify Relationships between TS% and Zone Volumes¶

In [38]:

Regression Findings: Shot Mix as the Primary Engine¶

The regressions confirm what the eye already suspects from the plot: shot mix, by itself, explains most of the league’s efficiency boom.

  • A +1 percentage-point bump in three-point volume lifts league TS% by $\approx$ +0.23 pp

    • (slope = 0.2337, $r = 0.92$, $R^2 \approx 0.85$, $p < 0.001$)

  • A 1 pp drop in mid-range volume raises TS% by $\approx$ +0.27 pp

    • (slope = –0.2691, $r = –0.93$, $R^2 \approx 0.86$, $p < 0.001$)

In other words, more threes and fewer long twos account for roughly four-fifths of the year-to-year movement in league-wide true shooting—even before we factor in pace, accuracy gains, or defensive adjustments.

Rim frequency remains steady, acting as an efficiency anchor while the perimeter trade-off drives the scoring surge. These results quantify the core analytics doctrine—arc-or-rim over mid-range—and set the stage for the next section, where we test whether rising shooting accuracy and tempo add explanatory power beyond this revamped shot diet.

Section Recap — Shot Mix $\rightarrow$ Efficiency¶

By joining league-level shot-zone shares (three_rate, mid_rate) with the season-average True Shooting % from Advanced.csv, we tracked three decades of change in one frame. The visual tells the headline story: three-point volume climbs past 40%, mid-range volume falls below 30%, and league TS% rises from ~.50 to ~.56. Regression pins down the causality.

  • Each +1 pp shift toward threes boosts TS% by $\approx$ +0.23 pp ($r = 0.92$, $R^2 \approx 0.85$, $p < 0.001$).
  • Each –1 pp shift away from mid-range lifts TS% by $\approx$ +0.27 pp ($r = –0.93$, $R^2 \approx 0.86$, $p < 0.001$).

Together, these two swaps explain about 80% of the year-to-year jump in league-wide efficiency, while rim frequency stays constant as a high-value anchor.

The takeaway is clear: the NBA’s scoring boom isn’t just faster pace or better shooters; it’s chiefly the deliberate reallocation of attempts from long twos to threes. This proves that the “arc-or-rim” doctrine is the driving engine of modern offensive success and the foundation for the next layers of analysis on accuracy and tempo.

15) Project Summary: The NBA’s Data-Driven Evolution¶

Over the last quarter-century, the NBA has transformed from a traditional, paint-focused league into a fast-paced, perimeter-oriented spectacle. By combining player–level advanced metrics, team aggregate summaries, and spatial shot–location data, this project has charted how strategic emphasis has shifted, what has driven those shifts, and how the game might continue to evolve.

Key Findings¶

The most striking change is the league’s embrace of long-range offense. Three-point attempts have become the focal point of team strategies, replacing midrange jumpers as the primary scoring option. This shift has forced defenses to extend outward, creating new driving lanes and changing the fundamental geometry of the court.

Improved spacing has yielded notable gains in scoring efficiency. As teams spread the floor and prioritized open looks, both rim attempts and three-point shots contributed to higher overall points per possession. In this environment, shot quality has become more important than sheer volume, and lineups are constructed to maximize open-look opportunities.

Another hallmark of the modern NBA is the blurring of traditional positions. Bigs now handle and shoot from distance, while smaller wings switch onto multiple assignments defensively. This “positionless” approach has expanded roster versatility and introduced new lineup configurations that capitalize on hybrid skill sets.

Finally, early adopters of these trends often reaped immediate benefits. Teams that embraced high three-point volume or experimented with unconventional spacing lineups saw rapid improvements in efficiency, demonstrating that data-backed innovations can quickly reshape competitive standards across the league.

Looking Ahead¶

As data collection and analytical tools continue to advance, teams will refine micro-adjustments to spacing, rotation, and lineup construction, seeking even the smallest edge. The ongoing rise in three-point attempts may prompt novel defensive countermeasures—such as switch-heavy schemes and length-focused personnel—to mitigate perimeter threats. Positionless basketball will further erode the guard-forward-center distinctions, rewarding organizations that prioritize versatile athletes capable of multiple roles. And future rule changes or new tracking technologies will create fresh inflection points, requiring continuous analytical monitoring to stay ahead.

By documenting these patterns and anticipating emerging tendencies, this project provides a roadmap for coaches, front offices, and league officials to navigate—and help shape—the next chapter of basketball’s strategic evolution.
